That in the opinion of this House, the preferential tariff should only apply to importations through Canadian seaports.
He said : Mr. Speaker, this notice of motion has been standing in my name on the order paper for some weeks, and I have been in hopes that the government might adopt the policy which is enunciated in it, but now that the buuget has been brought down my hopes are disappointed in that regard. I cannot hope therefore to have the policy adopted during the present session ; but, believing as I do that it is in the best interests of Canada that this policy should be adopted at another session of parliament, I crave the indulgence of the House for a few moments while I give my humble views as to why this policy should be adopted in Canada.
Some one may ask : Where is the demand for such legislation from any public body ? There have been many resolutions passed by boards of trade and other bodies, and one I believe by a provincial legislature, asking that such legislation be enacted. I have in my hand a resolution passed unanimously by the Halifax Board of Trade as far back as February 25, 1901. That resolution was communicated by telegraph to the Hon. W. S. Fielding, as follows :
Resolved that this council cordially endorses the suggestion of a member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which provides that the customs rebate of thirty-three and one third per cent on goods manufactured in Great Britain be allowed only when said goods are landed at Canadian ports, and pledges itself to use every means in its power to urge the adoption of the measure by the government.
In the month of August, 1901, a conference of the boards of trade of the maritime provinces, held at Chatham, N.B., passed the following resolution :
Resolved, that in the opinion of this board the preferential customs tariff as applied to imports from Great Britain should only apply to goods imported directly through Canadian ports.
At a conference of all the Canadian boards of trade, held at Toronto in June, 1902, this matter was very thoroughly discussed. A resolution favouring it was moved by a gentleman from St. John. After a considerable amount of discussion, the resolution was amended on motion of Mr. Munro, of Montreal, and the following resolution was passed unanimously :
In order to encourage the importation of British goods via Canadian ports, this conference desires that the preferential rebate on goods imported from Great Britain arriving by United States ports shall be limited to 25 per cent.
Many able arguments were made at that conference on behalf of the original reso-

iution. If you will allow me, I will quote from a speech delivered by Mr. Gaskin, of Kingston. He said :
I was more than surprised when I heard that the Dominion government made a preferential tariff on goods coming from England and did not stipulate they should come through Canadian ports. I remember, a number of years ago. that Canadian boats were allowed to carry grain from Chicago and Milwaukee to Port Col-borne. That grain went over the Welland road to Port Dalhousie ; it was taken by Canadian boat from Port Dalhousie and brought to Oswego. The Americans tried to stop that, and they have stopped everything since that was of benefit to our Canadian boats. I remember a number of years ago when I was captain of a steamer, just after the American war, I went into the port of Cleveland to report at the custom house, and they presented me with a bill of $140 or $150, and what do you suppose that was for ? For a war tax in the United States. That is the treatment we have been receiving from a Canadian standpoint, and I do certainly say the government made a great mistake in allowing that preferential tariff to apply to merchandise coming through the United States.
I will also quote from a speech delivered by Mr. George E. Drummond, who afterwards became, and now is, the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Mr. Drummond said :
It is a shame that we should permit our exports from Canada, from the west and from the centre of Canada, to go out via American ports if we can send them by Canadian ports. There is no question, as Mr. Gaskin said, that if you can fill these boats both ways that will mean cheaper freight rates for the men of the west, and that our rail-ways will meet us in a generous spirit I am perfectly confident, if the volume of trade will permit of it. For that reason I propose to support this motion. My friend from Windsor has spoken of what the Americans might do. I tell you that when the Americans meet in such a conference as this, they do not care very much what Canadians are going to do. They believe in themselves. We in this country have never had confidence in ourselves ; our banks would not be laden down with $250,000,000 earning three per cent if our people had confidence enough to develop Canadian transportation and develop Canadian mines.

Wilkie, of Toronto, spoke as follows :
We have granted this privilege of preferential tariff in favour of British goods, and it was said at the time that we did this we would suffer for it, the Americans would retaliate. What have they done ? ' You are really getting on to our game, you are finding us out.'" I know leading protectionists of the United States, and they told me plainly, 'You do not know how to manage your own affairs, do not be afraid of us. Our whole policy is not dictated by a desire to injure Canada. We have our own business 'to look after, and you are only a small factor in the matter. We are not doing this to injure you, we are doing it to benefit ourselves.' Let us tjnnk the same way, let us benefit ourselves. As to the argument of Mr. Saunders, that he was forced to export his goods by way of Bos-Mr. LOGAN.
ton or New York, what does that mean? It means that owing to our allowing this preference on British goods coming through Boston and New York, instead of limiting it to goods that come only through Halifax, St. John, Quebec and -Montreal, he was forced to send his goods to Boston and New York. But force them to bring our goods through Canadian ports and you will have cheaper freight rates for Canadian produce from your own ports. I do not think we should give way in this matter. Retaliation is a barbarous word, and it is not followed out except we want to injure, and we are not going to injure the United States, and as long as we are going to benefit ourselves, we should consider ourselves.
I will not weary the House by reading any further from that*report. Shipping is certainly one of the greatest industries of any country, and to encourage the shipping industry is to encourage the building up of the nation. To build up a nation it is important to make it a maritime nation ; and in order to do that, we should assist in building up maritime ports. In this country we are doing a great deal for the west. As a representative from the east, I am willing that we should spend large sums of money in developing the west as the future granary of the world ; but we should not forget that there is an east as well as a west. It may be said that we are selfish in asking this. I claim that we are not selfish. This is a broad national question, and the people of the west should be willing to assist us in bringing goods to the maritime ports and building up Canada as a whole.	[DOT]
Now, what are the objections to this proposition ? The first is that it would increase freight rates. At the present time the freight rates fronj Great Britain to Winnipeg are the same via St. John as they are via New York, Boston or Portland. I do not see any reason why they should be increased. It is said that if we gave the freight to Canadian lines, they would increase the freight rates. That is not saying much for their patriotism, but if they showed a disposition to do so, we could hold this over them as a lever, to see that they did not. I am sure that with the number of lines running between Canada and Great Britain, there would be sufficient competition to keep the freight rates down to a reasonable level. At the present time, one of the great difficulties of Canadian shipping lines is that they do not receive a return cargo. Last year we sent $131,000,000 worth of goods to Great Britain, and of that amount we sent over $41,000,000 through United States ports, while our ships were going from Canadian ports half laden to British ports. This is not Canad-ianism ; it is not a national spirit ; and if we can do anything to encourage a Canadian, national spirit in this country, we should do so, and do so at the earliest opportunity.

It is said that we have not facilities at Canadian ports. We shall never have those facilities unless we encourage Canadian ports to provide them ; and it is the duty of this government to assist them to provide facilities for shipping goods inwards ox-outwards. The argument has been .used that we have not the facilities. I have here a letter from a member of the great pioneer steamship line of Canada, Mr. Andrew Allan. In a letter I had written to Mr. Allen I stated it was claimed that more rapid transit could be secured via New York than by the St. Lawrence route, and Mr. Allan in reply says :
I maintain, that as far as our Liverpool steamers are concerned, we are now in a position to deliver traffic to Canadian houses as rapidly by our routes as can be done by any United States port.
Mr. Allan should be in a position to speak on this matter.
A further objection to this legislation which has been raised is that by it we may offend the United States, that the legislation is too drastic as against the United States. I do not admit that Mr. Speaker, and even if the legislation is drastic as against the United States it would be only adopting the United States policy. The historic policy of the United States has been along these lines. If Great Britain had adopted the policy adopted by the United States as far as coasting law is concerned, she would have paralysed the shipping industries of that country years ago. For the past one hundred years the United States has extended its navigation laws to all its outlying possessions. As early as 1817, under President Madison, Congress first provided that commerce between the territories and possessions of the United States should be regarded as coastwise and confined to vessels built in the United States, officered by the United States citizens and flying the United States flag. This policy has been continued from that time down to the present day. Whenever territories are annexed to the United States suitable legislation has extended this policy to embrace within the provisions of the coasting laws, trade with the newly acquired territories. In 1808 the navigation laws as to transportation of merchandise were extended to Alaska. In an Act approved of April 12, 1900, dealing with Porto Rico, it is provided in section 9 as follows :
That the commissioner of navigation shall make such regulations, subject to the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, as he may deem expedient for the nationalization of all vessels owned by the inhabitants of Porto Rico on the eleventh day of April, eighteen hundred and ninety-nine, and which continued to be so owned up to the date of such nationalization, and for the admission of the same to all the benefits of the coasting trade of the United States ; and the coasting trade between Porto Rico and the United States shall be regulated
in accordance with the provisions of law applicable to such trade between any two great coasting districts of the United States.
By an Act in reference to Hawaii approved April 30, 1900, it is provided :
That all vessels carrying Hawaiian registers on the twelfth day of August, eighteen hundred and ninety-eight, and which -were owned bona fide by citizens of the United States, or the citizens of Hawaii, together with the following named vessels claiming Hawaiian register-
Naming the vessels.
-shall be entitled to be registered as American vessels, with the benefits and privileges appertaining thereto, and the coasting trade between the islands aforesaid and any other portion of the United States, shall be regulated in accordance with the provisions of law applicable to such trade between any two great coasting districts.
They have extended their coasting laws half way across the Pacific and taken in the Hawaiian Islands. Later on they secured possession of the Philippine islands, at the antipodes, many many thousand miles away, and in spite of the fact that their tariff law is as stringent against the Philippine islands as against any other country ^except for a preference of 25 per cent, and in spite of the fact that they require the Philippine islanders to sell them hemp without the tax of $7.50 a ton, which is charged upon hemp sent to Canada, they have extended the coasting laws of the United States half way around the world to embrace the Philippines. Are we then to be told in Canada that we cannot adopt a policy to encourage Canadian ports and the shipment of Canadian goods by Canadian lines for fear of offending the United States of America ? Let me read the Act in reference to the Philippine islands, and I will ask members of the House to pay particular attention to section 2. It is Bill No. S 2259, United States Congress, and is as follows :
Be it enacted that on and after July 1st, 1905, no merchandise except supplies for army and navy shall be transported by sea under penalty of forfeiture thereof, between ports of the United States and ports or places in the Philippine archipelago directly or via a foreign port or for any part of the voyage in any other vessel than a vessel of the United States.
On section 2.
That on and after July 1st, 1905, no foreign vessel shall transport passengers between ports of the United States and ports or places in the Philippine archipelago either directly or by way of a foreign port under a penalty of $200 for each passenger so transported and landed,
In other words, if a Canadian vessel should carry any passengers or freight from a port in the United tSates, to the Philippine islands, one of the possessions of the United States, that freight would be liable to for-

feiture, and the boat to a fine of $200 for each passenger carried.
By the Cuban customs regulations, 1901, it is provided : that coastwise trade can only be exercised by Cuban vessels or those of the United States, so far as it relates to the transportation of merchandise.
That, Sir, is the legislation of the United States of America. The United States of America have built themselves up largely because they believe in themselves, are proud of their country and dare to legislate for their country irrespective of what other countries think or do.
We have to a somewhat limited extent adopted this policy of giving a preference to Canadian seaports. In item 608 of the tariff tea and ground coffee imported direct from the place of production, and tea and ground coffee purchased in bond in the United Kingdom are admitted free, otherwise a duty of 10 per cent is charged upon them. In item S7 of the tariff, salt from the United Kingdom or any British possession is admitted free, otherwise there is a duty varying from 5 to 7i cents per 100 pounds. In the treaty with France we provide that the goods must be transported direct from France to Canada and not by way of any other country. To that extent we have adopted this policy. It is legislation it seems to me, along the right lines, legislation along Canadian lines, to build up Canada, to build up Canadian seaports. We have gone a long distance towards giving a preference to the motherland ; let us in giving a preference to the motherland, give a preference to the ports of the Dominion of Canada and let us while we say ' Canada for the Canadians ' adopt the policy of ' Canadian seaports for Can-adihn imports.'

FIELDING (Minister of Fi-nance(. I#am glad my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has to-day brought forward this motion of which he gave notice some time ago, not that I expect that it can be adopted immediately as part of the budget of this year,-and I do not suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Logan) now expects that,-but I feel that it is a subject on which discussion may do much good. It is a subject on which there is need of education, not only outside of the House, but, possibly inside the House. I am aware that possibly, from some points of view, objections may be raised to the motion of my hon. friend. But, for my own part I am heartily in favour of it, and, if he decides to divide the House upon it, I shall have pleasure in giving my vote in support of the motion. For the purposes of the present budget and the present condition of affairs we cannot deal with it. But I hope there will be such an educational movement on the question that, at no distant day, we may adopt it as part of our practical legislation. If that can be done at no distant day no one will rejoice more than I shall.

I think that the reasons my hon. friend has given in support of his motion are strong, and I believe that the more the subject is discussed, the more likely we are to reach the conclusion that he has reached after so much consideration. So, while I do not say. that his motion will receive the assent of the House, to take effect at once, it is a move in the right direction. Even if it is not received with unanimous approval, as I would desire to see it received, I trust that the time will soon come when we may accept it as part of a thoroughly national policy. But it is certainly a subject upon which discussion is desirable and education is necessary. I congratulate my hon. friend upon having given it the attention he has, and I repeat that, if it is necessary for his purpose to divide the House upon it, I will cordially vote in support of the motion.

It is certainly cheering to see the Minister of Finance condemning himself and his government-for that is what his speech amounted to. He and his colleagues have had, and now have, power in their hands to carry out the spirit of this motion, and yet they have failed to do it. He admits the injustice done to Canada, and declares that he knows that wrong is done, but only says that if the House will give its sanction he does not know but that he will deal with it to the future. But, though they have had it in their power to do justice in Canada they have refrained from doing it. What their reason may be is not known to us-it is for those hon. gentlemen to explain. And it seems to me that the hon. member (Mr. Logan) who moved this motion is also worthy of censure. He has had this notice of motion on the paper for weeks. What would naturally be his object in putting it on the paper but to bring the attention of the government and of this House to the need of the change he proposes, with a view to having the government deal wi,th it in connection with the tariff ? Had it been brought forward in time, and a favourable expression of opinion from the House secured, the Finance Minister might fairly have been expected to take note of it and act upon it when he brought down his budget. But the hon. gentleman, though putting a notice upon the paper seems to have allowed the time to pass, and did not bring it forward until now after the budget speech has been delivered. And then the minister congratulates him on what he has done and declares that if the hon. gentleman presses his motion to a division he will vote for it. That is a_wonderful admission on the part of the government, and a most amusing one. I am glad to notice that at last, though late, there are some members on that side who are not prevented from expressing

tlieir views on this question by fear ot offending the United States. This everlasting cringing to the United States that we have had exemplified by members of the Reform Party during the whole time that I have been in this House, now twenty-six years, has been humiliating to every Canadian, and, if possible, more humiliating to representatives of Canada in this House. When any matter of a similar nature to this was brought before the House and it was recommended that we should take practical steps, what was generally the answei' from the other side? These hon. gentlemen told us not to exasperate the Americans or the Americans would retaliate. For twenty years we were told that by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in regard to our proposal to prevent the Americans taking away our logs, but to compel them to manufacture them into lumber on this side. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) told us that the Americans would retaliate, that they would double the lumber duties, that they would prevent us from marketing our lumber-in fact that they would desfroy us if we attempted co stand up for our own interest. And we have the hon. member for South Oxford (Sir Richard Cartwright) declaring that the whole trend of the Conservative policy was to keep the Americans in a state of annoyance and so prevent us from securing a reciprocity treaty. And we were assured that the sunny ways of the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when brought to bear upon the obdurate hearts of the Americans, would cause them to see the selfishness of their ways and amend. And that right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) signalized his entrance into office by the declaration that, to soften the hearts of the Americans and secure a reciprocity treaty, he was willing to give away all our fishing privileges on the Atlantic. But there was a sudden and unexpected howl from the maritime provinces, and we have heard nothing more of the right hon. gentleman's proposal since then. But he did everything possible to please the Americans ; the commission went into Washington to soften their hearts and bring them to a sense of their duty. But it was found to be labour in vain, like washing a nigger to make him white. At last we have come to the conclusion that it is better to look after ourselves. X often asked myself when we might hope the hon. gentlemen opposite would reach that conclusion, and they seem to have awakened to the truth at last. AY hat are hon. gentlemen sent here for ? Not to legislate for the United States, but to legislate for Canada.
I am glad that one member on that side has at last found courage to declare that he is in favour of looking after the interest of Canada in this matter. It would be
amusing, if it were not humiliating, to hear the answer of the Minister of Finance. That hon. gentleman says he will vote for the motion. He will vote in favour of doing a thing that he could have done by legislation long ago. The people will understand that, and they will judge of the hon. gertleman's sincerity.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) who has just resumed his seat has always a way of his own in a debate of this kind. In his speech he did not refer to the advantage that would accrue to Canada from the adoption of the policy enunciated in this resolution.
I took it for granted that no member of parliament was so wanting in common sense that he would for a moment doubt the advantage of it.

I am glad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is in favour of this resolution. The objections to it that he raises might be removed by passing a Bill only to take effect from a certain time. We have the Intercolonial to St. John, and also from Montreal to Halifax, and we have in prospect, at no distant day, that great railway that is going to run from ocean to ocean. And we expect that in the winter season the trade of China and Japan to Britain and other European ports will go over that line, and that the trade from Great Britain and the continent of Europe to Oriental countries will also pass over it. But that is a question that we may leave to the future. We can be in favour of building up our own ports, the ports of Quebec and Montreal in summer and of Halifax and St. John in winter ; and I think we should all agree as one man to support this resolution, to take effect at some time that would not be detrimental to the present budget or its operation in any way. I am certainly in favour of this resolution, and I hope that some good will come out of it at no distant date.

It appears to me that this matter is of too much importance to be relegated to any single private individual of the House. When you begin by law to say that nothing shall be imported into Canada from Great Britain except it comes through Canadian ports, it is too violent an interference with traffic to meet with my approval on so sudden a presentation of the case. I think the people who have their money invested in steamships and railways and who are prepared to bring goods and deliver them in Canada at the cheapest price, are, entitled to some consideration, and so are the consumers of this country. If we by law force all dutiable! goods from Great Britain to come by Canadian ships and through Canadian ports,

it will unquestionably have the effect of increasing the value of those goods to the consumers. I say it is a matter of too much importance to be considered so hastily, and I assume that before a change of such magnitude is made it will be brought in by the government itself.

I had hoped to get through with this session, Mr. Speaker, without your having to hear my voice, but. we have had such an exhibition of insincerity on the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that I cannot keep silent any longer. When the Finance Minister was advocating the building of a railroad from the Northwest down to the sea-board he assured gentlemen on this side of the House that the patriotism of Canadians would lead them to send their goods to Canadian ports in preference to American ports. The present exhibition will confirm, the opinion that there is no sin-; cerity whatever in any of the motions brought up by gentlemen on that side of the House. I can tell the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Logan) that many merchants bring all their goods to this country through Canadian ports, and do not allow their goods to come through United States ports so far as they can help it. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) says the effect of this resolution will be" to make goods dearer. All I can say is that I bring all the goods I can to this country through Canadian ports, and I manage to compete with other people pretty well.

I did not say it made them dearer, but it would make them dearer if they were compelled by law to come through Canadian ports.
. Mr. BROCK. I am sure the Finance Minister will give me credit for patriotism, not that I think it makes much difference, but because the Finance Minister has insisted that the farmers of the Northwest will be induced by patriotism to bill their grain 1 to Canadian ports.

I would like to see him take hold of it with the same energy that he manifested with regard to the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific to Moncton. In that ease he forced the government at the point of the bayonet to fall in with his wishes ; why should he not now be just as sincere in favour of Halifax and St. John as he was in favour of Moncton ? I congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) on the manner in which he has brought forward arguments in favour of this resolution. So far as the city I represent is concerned, I feel it would be a very great advantage indeed to the port of St. John if this resolution were adopted and carried into effect by legislation. During last year, the exports from the port of St. John, totalled $15,364,735, while the imports only amounted to $5,658,281. Some mention has been made of the rates at which freight is carried both by land and sea. I would like to state, Mr. * Speaker, that a reduction of the rates over

the ocean can only be effected by having full cargoes both ways. In the winter, steamers got out from St. John with full cargoes but they come back with very small cargoes. That trouble is grad-uajly lessening, but at the same time the business is still too one-sided. In order to have a lower freight rate, which would at the same time be a paying rate, for steamers as well as for railways, there must be cargoes both ways. We have heard complaints from time to time that the Intercolonial lias not been paying, and there have also been complaints that the Canadian Pacific Railway has not been doing a paying business from the port of St. John. If this resolution were carried into effect, there is no doubt in the world that the increase of business would be so great, both for the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and their connections in the maritime provinces, that the era of deficits, at least so far as the Intercolonial is concerned, would be brought to a speedy close.
The hon. member for Cumberland has spoken of the views which Canadians generally should entertain in regard to building up of all the ports of Canada. We are all interested, apart from where we may happen to live, in this matter because the success of one part of Canada tends to increase the success of the whole. There is no doubt that the St. Lawrence ports of Montreal and Quebec are equally interested in the successful carrying out of this proposition with the ports on the Atlantic sea-board. Its advantages are not altogether confined to the ports of Halifax and St. John. There are other fine ports which, as business comes to them, will increase and the carrying out of this proposition will be a decided advantage to the sections of the country interested in these ports. I do not think there is any argument in regard to the possibility of offending the United States. As a matter of fact at the present time we are treating the United States in a far more friendly way than they are treating us. We are taking from them a much greater proportion of imports than we are exporting to the United States. We have kept our tariff low against the United States while their tariff is high against us. So that, without any further remarks, I hope that the hon. gentleman who has introduced this resolution will ask for a division of the House upon it so that we can see what the sentiment of hon. members of this House in connection with this very important matter is. Then, I hope if the reply is favourable that the hon. Minister of Finance, who has expressed himself so much in favour of this idea, will take steps to have the resolution crystallized into law.

Mr. Speaker, before this debate comes to a close
I just wish to say a word or two upon this subject. It seems to me that this is rather a drastic measure, because you are undertaking to say to the merchant how he shall ship his goods whether they be going outward or inward. The merchant has difficulties enough to contend with without having to surmount such a difficulty as that. When we have given a preference to goods coming from Great Britain I would not like to see that limited in any way whatever. Let me give an illustration of how this works on outward bound goods and it will apply equally well to goods coming into this coun-trv. In our section of the country we buy large quantities of pease and rye. We get just as large a quantity of these goods into our warehouses to ship before the dose of navigation as we can. The moment navigation closes, down goes the price of grain two cents a bushel as a general thing. A few years ago when we were buying pease and rve the price dropped as usual at the close of navigation. Withifl a fortnight after the close of navigation arrangements were made so that we could ship our grain by rail to Boston and, ship it from that port. We got a lower rate than we ever got before. The consequence was that we increased the price that we were paying to our farmers by two cents a bushel and we gave them the same price that they were getting before navigation closed. If a law had been passed obliging us to export our goods by Canadian ports the farmers would have lost two cents a bushel on; every bushel of pease and rye that we purchased after the close of navigation. I wish to draw the attention of the House to this, and I also desire to point out, that this is a matter that will work both ways. It applies to exports and it implies to imports. I would like to consider this proposition very carefully before supporting it. I go for taking the shackles off trade, and relieving trade just as far as you can from1 any of its difficulties because I believe that the freer we are in our intercourse, the better it will be for us. Something has, been said about the way the United States treats us and the way we treat the United States. How did we treat the United States last year when they took the duty off coal ? Hid we do the same thing ? We kept it on; they took it off. I have nothing further to say nt the nresent time.
Mr. Speaker, we find in the ranks of the government party that there is still one free trader. I doubt if there is another one.
The hon. member for Victoria, N.S. (Mr. Ross).

I question very much about that hon. gentleman. I think that his party fealty is too strong. But, we have one hon. gentleman who is a free trader.

He does not seem to realize just what this debate Is about. He talks about the importation of pease and rye in connection with the preferential tariff. However, it is not a very unusual thing to find a Liberal member of parliament not knowing very much about the subject of the debate. I was very much surprised that the hon. minister of
Finance (Mr. Fielding) did not give us some reason he was so much in favour of this resolution which we are discussing and why he did not include this in his budget when he brought it down to this House. The hon. gentleman has expressed himself as very strongly in favour of this proposition, he is prepared to vote for it, but he gave us no reasons why he was not in favour of it when he brought down his budget proposals to this House ? Why is it ? What is the explanation of this sudden conversion ? Has the light suddenly burst upon the hon. gentleman's mind ? Has he only been converted since hearing the speech of the hon. member for Cumberland which was a very good speech although there was nothing in it in the way of inspiration ? Is it only since he heard the speech of the hon. member for Cumberland that he has become so strongly in favour of the proposition contained in this resolution ? It seems to me that if the hon. gentleman had not been trying to commit a patent fraud-I use the word not in its offensive sense-upon the country he would have given us some reason why he was compelled to forego the carrying out of the desire of his heart, some reason which prevented him from bringing in this proposal in his budget speech. Now, Sir, for my part I would like to hear some reasons given why this proposition should not be adopted by this parliament. I think the reasons given by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) and for South Renfrew (Mr. Wright) why this proposition should not be adopted were not such as to commend themselves to this House. This it seems to me would be a simple matter of justice to the ports of this country applying more particularly as it does to the Atlantic ports If the necessary facilities are not to be found at these ports now for the proper handling of this trade the government which has so much money to spend, which has so many millions to fritter away in little works where tliey are of no use to the general public might spend some of these millions to provide the ports of Halifax, St. John, Montreal and Quebec with the necessary facilities for handling this trade, and if it does it will be doing more for the benefit of the country than by giving away this monev to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, that is the view which I have taken of this question and I say that we in the maritime provinces who have made very e-rent sacrifices for the benefit of Canada are entitled to some return and if the hon. Minister of Finance had at heart the welfare' of the Mr. FOWLER.
maritime province from which he comes he would do more than express his opinion as to this proposition; he would crystallize this resolution into such legislation as would bring about the end desired.
Right Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister/. My hon. friend from Grev (Mr. Sproule) has failed this time, as he has failed at other times, to rightly appreciate the sense of the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the attitude of the government upon this question. I am not at all surprised at this and I do not think he himself is surprised ; I am afraid it is a constitutional defect with him. He saw at once the shadow of the United States falling on the path of this question. That is not where the difficulty lies.

I was only referring to the argument of the hon. member (Mr. Logan) that we should not refrain from doing this for fear of the United States. That is an argument which should not be used in this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well we have tried sunny ways with the United States and we have failed, and we have adopted another method which has not- been appreciated by gentlemen on the other side. The moment we found that our efforts for friendly trade relations with our neighbours did not materialize, and that our sunny ways had no effect on them, we thought we would try another policy, and we resolved among other things to build a transcontinental railway which would have the effect of increasing our trade to and from Great Britain over Canadian routes. Upon the general principle of this resolution there cannot be any difference of opinion. Even my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Wright) does not dissent from the proposition involved in the motion, and the argument which he adduced simply was, that until we had more accommodation for shipping in our ports we had to use Boston and other American ports. In my judgment at all events, the way to have better facilities and accommodation in our own harbours, is to turn as far as possible all our trade to these harbours. But there is another side to this question, and it is one which my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) does not appreciate. The hon. gentleman does not appreciate that this is a business government-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does not appreciate that we took before we leap, and that we try to ascertain where we will land before we attempt to jump. There is no doubt whatever that present the trade of Canada is every day running more and more into Canadian channels. The importations via the United

States are less this year, and my Information is that they are constantly decreasing all the time. The wholesale merchants bring almost all their importations to Canadian harbours, and according to the statistics of this year out of our total importation from Great Britain only a little over 30 per cent went to American ports. It was not so some few years ago. The day is not far distant, and my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) remembers it, when more than half of all the imports into Canada came by American ports We have been able through several successive years to change this, and to cause more imports and more exports to go and come through Canada. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) knows perfectly well that while at present most of the wholesale houses import through Canadian harbours, I understand that the retail business in Toronto, and Montreal, and London and Hamilton, is still largely done through United . States ports. The retail houses wish to have their orders filled in a hyrry ; they cable for their goods and they give instructions to send them by the cheapest-not by the cheapest, but by the quickest route-so that they may have them at the earliest opportunity. This is a circumstance which we have to look into. 1 think it is possible even in that case to force trade into Canadian channels. By giving due notice to importers of all classes, that they will get the British preference if [DOT]they send their importations by way of Canada, we should, I think, accomplish that. But, if without giving notice of the policy which the government intend to pursue on this question, we at once adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule), there probably would be a greater deal of disturbance caused in certain jines ot business. Far better is it that there should be no disturbance of that kind, and that such contemplated changes should be duly heralded so that all parties may take notice of it and act accordingly. Therefore, I think it is quite proper that this discussion should take place, and that all parties should understand that the government would be actuated and guided by it, as to what its future course should be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is not the first we have heard of this proposal. Did not my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) give notice of it last year, and if I remember correctly the year before. At all events the matter was before the House last year, and although the discussion upon it was imminent on many occasions, it has not been brought forward until now. The right hon. the Prime Minister has treated us to some rather unusual statements. His Minister of Finance told us at once that he was absolutely in favour of this motion, and the Prime Minister says the government will be in favour of it at some future time, because it is a business government and must make inquiry. But the Minister of Finance being in favour of it at once, he therefore cannot be a business minister. Possibly, however, the Minister of Finance is in favour of the motion and in favour of not acting upon it. Perhaps in that way his position can be reconciled with that of the right hon. gentleman. Although this question has been before the House for years and although it is now brought before the government by one of its most prominent supporters from the maritime provinces, it is remarkable there has not been an opportunity long, beJ fore this to make the inquiry to which the' right hon. gentleman refers. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is so impressed by the advantages of this motion, that he is ready, to vote for it to-day, even if the House is divided, and even, I suppose if the Prime Minister votes against it. If the Finance Minister has been so much impressed with the advantages of this policy, it does seem a little remarkable that we have had the discussion postponed until* this late date, and that the government have not yet made that inquiry which the< Prime Minister says is necessary. One would think that a measure such as that proposed would not create any great disturbance of trade, and I certainly believe it would be very much in the interests of the maritime provinces. But I would be inclined to go a little further than my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan). I do not see any reason why we should restrict the enactment to goods entered under the preferential tariff. If the principle is good, and the Minister of Finance says it is, why should we not simply provide that goods imported through Canadian ports whether under the preferential tariff or otherwise, should have more favourable treatment, so far as our customs tariff is concerned than if they came through United States ports. That would be dealing with the matter from a general standpoint, and would not be restricting the operation of the proposal to a certain class of imports. If it is advisable to make this discrimination with regard to goods imported from Great Britain, why should we not make exactly the same discrimination in regard to goods imported from Germany, or from France, or from* Belguim, or any other country ? If the principle is good, and the Minister of Finance thinks it is, so far as British trade is concerned, why is it not equally good so' far as trade from other countries beyond the sea is concerned? The same object is to be achieved, viz. : the building up of our Canadian ports by bringing importations to this country through them. I would think that the motion should not stop short of that point.
I submit further for the consideration of the government that if they really do in-

tend to deal with this subject, and not simply to allow this motion to pass as a mere matter of form, the government would simply have one of two alternatives; either to carry out the declared will of parliament or to resign. It will only take about four words in the tariff Act to carry out what my hon. friend (Mr. Logan) suggests and it can be done in five minutes by any ordinary draughtsman. I do not understand that this is a matter upon which the government is not to have a policy ; I do not understand that this is a matter upon which the Finance Minister can vote one way and the Prime Minister another, and that the cabinet can leave the matter absolutely free to be dealt with, or not to be dealt with at all. If this House declares in favour of the resolution of my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) or if my suggestion is carried out, the tariff ought to be amended at once, and it can be done by the insertion of two sentences in the Customs Act. I do not think this is a subject with which we should play by way of passing a motion, which may mean something or mean nothing. If the words of the Finance Minister mean anything, they mean that the chief financial exponent of the government is-in favour of a policy that can be put into force in the simplest possible way during the present session. That is the position in which the matter presents itself to my mind.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister says that the government has tried sunny ways with the United States, and it has failed. There can be no doubt about that.
I do not know that they have tried any other ways up to the present time,; because I observe that during the present year, at first they declined to extend the terms of an Order in Council permitting United States vessels to do the coasting trade between British Columbia and the Yukon, but at a later date, on the 29th March, they repent-; ed and United States vessels continue to do that trade, as they have done it during the last four or five years. Of course, I realize that there may be certain difficulties that present themselves to the government in connection with that trade.
One of the difficulties which the Prime Minister referred to-the difficulty in the retail trade of Canada-which might present itself if this policy were carried out, would probably not present itself at all if the government had been able to carry out the project of a fast Atlantic service ; because one reason why such a difficulty would occur is the lack of expeditious and cheap transportation from the mother country to Canada of such articles as would be' imported by retail merchants, not articles imported in great bulk such as are brought into this country by wholesale merchants. It is Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
very much to be regretted that the right hon. gentleman's government could not have seen fit to avoid meddling with the contract which was made by the government which preceded it. If this government had seen fit to carry out the arrangements then made, it is pretty certain that the fast Atlantic service would have been an accomplished fact long before this, and no such difficulty as that suggested by the Prime Minister this afternoon would have confronted us at this time. I agree fully with what my hon. friend from Cumberland has said as to the necessity of building up our maritime ports. When he informs us that more than $40,000,000 worth of our products went last year through American ports. I think he has placed before the House a very significant object lesson.

Will my hon. friend pardon me for a moment ? I think I have been misunderstood. The goods subject to the preference which were brought from England into Canada through American ports last year, amounted to nearly $15,000,000. The goods sent from Canada to Great Britain last year amounted to $131,202,098, of which $41,174,715 went through United States ports.

That is quite what I understood. I think that is a very significant object lession, and one which ought to make us doubly cautious, in carrying out any scheme of transportation in Canada, cautious that lest this be done in such a way as to maintain, or possibly increase, the ratio of the exportation of the products of Canada to Great Britain and to the continent of Europe by United States ports. I trust that this motion, if the government see fit to permit it to pass, will not be regarded as a mere idle form, but that the government will understand that the will of parliament has been expressed on this subject, and will proceed to carry out that will during the present session by making an amendment of a few words in the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When this Bill was before the committee a day or two ago, I suggested instead of clause 1, in the present form, to substitute two other clauses which I then read. At that time it was suggested by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that these clarfses might require some further consideration, and. since that time I have received a memorandum which in his absence I may perhaps be permitted to read to the House. He suggested that the first clause as suggested seemed to be right, but the second clause which refers to Chapter 119 was wrong, he said that except as to companies formed before August 11, 1899, that section was repealed by 2 Ed. VII Chap. 15. He suggested that I should omit the words ' to prevent ' in the amendment which I had proposed.
I have considered the objections made by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and I think that they are perfectly in order and that it would be proper to amend the Bill by substituting one section for the two now under consideration. My suggestion would be that instead of the two sections which I then proposed to substitute for the first section we should adopt the following :
To remove possible doubt it is hereby declared that the expression ' the construction and operation of railways or telegraph or telephones ' in section 5 of the Companies Act, 1902, does not include acting as a contractor, in railway, telegraph or telephone construction, and * the construction and working of railways ' in section 3 of the Companies Act, chapter 119, revised statutes of Canada, does not include acting as a contractor in railway construction.
I think this meets the difficulty suggested by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker).
What is the significance of that change ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the Companies Act of 1902 it is provided that incorporation by letters patent may be granted to any company for any of the purposes of objects to which the legislative authority of Canada is applicable, or rather extends, except the following :
Except the construction and working of railways or of telegraph or telephone lines or the business of banking, &c.
It appears that these words have been construed as applicable to companies incorporated for the purpose of constructing telephone and telegraph lines, for constructing railways, although they are simply contracting companies. It is in order to avoid that possible construction of the section in the present Act, that the present amendment is proposed, that is in order to gi|ve authority to incorporate by letters patent) Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
companies to construct railways, telegraph and telephone lines. That is the object of the present amending Bill as I understand it from my hon. friend from Essex (Mr. Cowan) and if that be the case then I see no objection to the amendment.

Some years ago we had a good deal of trouble arising through the operation of constructing companys formed for the purpose of building railways. It could hardily be said that the railway corporation formed itself into a construction company, but the same parties as were in the railway company, with one or two others, formed the construction company, and so manipulated the contracts as to secure the government bonuses and everything 'else possible for themselves. It did not turn out very creditably either to the parties or to the country. And I remember that a strong feeling was aroused against that method ot operation. It seems to me that this proposed amendment will allow the formation of these constructing companies ; and, when we consider the possibility of that in connection with the new transcontinental railway, it seems all the greater reason why we should avoid this danger.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may explain that my attention has not been drawn to any need for an amendment of the law as we have it. My only object was to try to give effect to what I understand to be the intention of the promoter of the Bill. But I have absolutely no interest in it, and have never been asked to introduce legislation of this kind-no representations have been made to the government, to my knowledge, in favour of such a change. I am quite willing that the matter should be postponed and dealt with hereafter if desired. If the hon. member who promotes the Bill is not sufficiently interested in it to be here when it comes up, I have no desire to press it.

I am not saying that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) wishes to press the matter. But I have heard a good deal of discussion on this subject before, and it seemed to me that this amendment was all the more worthy of attention because of the very important scheme for a transcontinental railway that is now before the country. I do not know whether this Bill is or is not intended to have any connection with that matter, but the circumstances might create suspicion that there was some other object in view than that which was given to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wish to make it clear that I have nothing whatever to do with the Bill, and that my interference is solely directed to trying to put the Bill in workable form. In order to prevent any doubt arising, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, so that the matter may be fully considered.

I do not see any possible objection to a company being formed to construct a railway, or a telephone, or a telegraph line. Surely these are things that a company could be properly formed for the purpose of doing.

In the cases to which 1 have referred, this state of things was shown : The railway company got a bonus from the government, then they formed a construction company, virtually of their own membership. They built the railway through contractors, but, though they got the bonuses, they did not pay the workmen and subcontractors in full.	.
Then when an effort was made to follow the matter, it was found that the money had been handed over to a company entirely outside of parliament, and one that we could not hold responsible, because, it was said, they were not the parties who were given the original charter as a railway company. So the parties in the construction company got the money, and those who did the work never were paid. Afterwards, I believe, parliament had to come to the rescue of some of the parties who had not been paid, and had to make provision for the payment of at least a portion of the debt. But the centre of the difficulty was the construction company, and it always seemed to me it was a very bad principle to allow the intervention of such companies. This amendment, being proposed at this particular time, naturally creates suspicion that what was done in past years will be repeated under this amendment.
Progress reported.

The gentlemen in the committee argued that because the Railway Commission had power to order protection to the highways my Bill was not necessary, because, if the Railway Commission ordered that protection, the railways would be bound to furnish it. Now the Act as it stands to-day does nothing of the kind. The Act requires railways only to fence or to protect. But the Supreme Court has decided that fencing means merely fencing the right of way up to the highway and stopping at the cattleguards, turning the fences in at right angles to the cattleguards and stopping there. That decision was made last November. True, the learned gentleman who was before the Railway Committee promised us that the case was going to the Privy Council, and that therefore it was not necessary to amend the law now. To begin with, that case does not come within the limits, because it is an Ontario case, and you have to have $4,000 in dispute in an Ontario case before you can take it to the Privy Council. I do not know whether it can possibly go there or not. But we must not assume that the Privy Council is going to overrule a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, nor can we assume that this House will override the Railway Committee, for instance. We presume, as the Minister of Justice indicates, that the decision of the Railway Committee is right, and he told me emphatically that the onus is on me to show wherein the Railway Committee is wrong. A statement that the case of McKay and the Grand Trunk is going to the Privy Council does not do us any good until we have evidence that the Privy Council has reversed the decision of the Supreme Court. Now it was argued in that case that the company had not properly fenced the railway because they had not properly protected the crossing, that fencing does not mean only up to the highway, or else the section was senseless, because it was dealing with the rate of speed and with the question of protection; and it was argued before the Supreme Court that it must have meant the kind of fencing as protecting, because the section was dealing with the rate of speed. But the Supreme Court has laid down that the fencing as described in the Act means nothing but a fence of the right of way as between adjoining proprietors. Now the present law requires that the railways must do that, or else they must protect, but they need not do both. But the Railway Committee paid no attention to that consideration. and I ask this House to pay some attention to it. My first amendment is that the word ' or ' should he struck out and the word ' and ' inserted. The effect would be to make the company provide both the fencing and the protection. The committee

thought that a protection ordered by the Railway Committee in a special case was better protection than a general law, which I am contending for. But X am trying to impress upon this House that as the law stands to-day no matter what the Railway Commission may order you would not have any protection according to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. Now the Supreme Court has decided two things : They have decided that fencing means fencing the right of way and turning into the cattle guards. Every one knows that is not protection whatever to people on the sidewalk or on the highway. In the second place, the Supreme Court decided that protection is such as is ordered by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council now replaced by the Railway Commission. Now even if the contention were correct that it is sufficient to have an order from the Railway Commission, still, unless you grant the first part of my amendment, striking out the word 'or' and putting in the word 'and' you have no protection. The railway company will say :	We are only
bound! to fence or to protect. We have fenced, and we were ordered to protect, but your statute limits the liability to fencing or protection. If we do one or the other we have done all that we are required to do. The statute only requires us to make an alternative for fencing, but not to do both. I do not think the members of this House should leave the law in its present uncertain state. The 214 members of this House are sent here to legislate in what they believe to be in the interests of the people, and they are better able to judge of that than any learned counsel who may be sent before the committee. It is not the duty of a railway lawyer to instruct the members of the House in their duty to their constituents. The contention of the counsel in the Railway Committee was that, if the commission ordered certain protection at a crossing that that was all that was required, and would be better than a general law. I say again that even if that contention were sound, still the first part of my amendment must be granted, or else the railway will not be liable for failing to afford sufficient protection.
I am satisfied that if we had read it more carefully last year when we were in committee for seven or eight weeks on this Bill, many of us pretty well tired of the Railway Bill, we would have understood the effect of it better than we did. I admit that those who were in the House taking part in the discussion upon the general consolidation of the railway law were tired and * being urged by other lion, gentlemen in the House to hurry up and get through with it, we did not notice the difference between the word ' or ' and ' and.' I would have contended for what I am contending for now had I noticed it. It was a mistake on

the part of the House. X think it was a mistake on the part of the then Minister of Railways and Canals. His attention was not drawn to it and he may have read it as if ' or ' meant ' and,' or he may have read it: as if the word ' or ' included both. The word ' or ' ought to be stricken out and the word 'and' be put in. It would be more satisfactory perhaps if I should pause and not say anything about the other matter until we consider the point as to whether we should not have the other protection which is provided for in addition to the fencing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Act as we now have it reads as follows :
227. No train shall pass in or through any thicklv peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten miles an hour unless the track is fenced or properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act, or unless permission is given by some regulation or order of the Board. The Board may limit such speed in any case to any rate which it deems expedient.
The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) is that between the word ' fenced ' and ' properly ' in the third line the word ' and ' should be substituted for the word ' or ' which would make the section read in this way :
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced and properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act.
This protection is proposed in addition to the fencing provided for by section 199 of the Railway Act which section provides that:
199. The company shall erect and maintain upon the railway fences, gates and cattle guards, as follows
(a)	Fences of a minimum height of four feet six inches on each side of the railway.
(b)	Swing gates in such fences, of the minimum height aforesaid, with proper hinges and fastenings, at farm crossings.
Then paragraph 2 provides that:
Such fences, gates and cattle guards shall be suitable and sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway.
My hon. friend proposes that in addition to these fences it would be necessary for the railway' company to provide protection in the manner prescribed by the Act because he proposes that the speed shall not be greater than ten miles an hour :
Unless the track is fenced and properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act.
Let me draw the attention of the committee to sections 184, 186 and 187 which sections provide that no railway may cross a highway unless upon leave first having been
obtained from the Railway Commission, which leave is made subject to such regulations as the Railway Commission shall see fit to adopt for the purpose of protection. Then, in respect to a railway which is al-i ready in existence upon application made by the town or village, under section 187, the board may order the railway company within a specified time to provide such protection as it thinks proper under the circumstances.
Why do you make it necessary for the people to make an application ? Why not have the law so that the railway is bound to take proper precautions without coming to the Railway Commission ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The railway company is bound to observe the law just as all other corporations are ? Section 25 provides that the Railway Commission may make such provisions as it deems proper :
With respect to the rolling stock, apparatus, cattle guards, appliances, signals, methods, devices, structures and works, to be used upon the railway so as to provide means for the due protection of property, the employees of the company and the public.
So that on the whole the provision of the Railway Act is that no railway can cross a highway without permission having first been obtained from the Railway Commission and that permission to cross the highway is made subject to such regulations as the board deems advisable under the circumstances to properly protect the public using the highway. In addition to that it a crossing already exists upon written application to the board, the board will make such provision in respect to any such crossing as is necessary for the protection of the public and the board may go, under section 25, to any length it deems proper and make any regulation it deems necessary. The board has full jurisdiction and control over any railway crossing that is not now in existence as well as those which are already in existence. The board will exercise its judgment in respect to any such crossing in view of the existing facts at a particular place, but if you adopt my hon. friend's suggestion what is the result going to be ? You will require at each crossing a fence, you will require in addition to that the protection provided for by the commissioners under the statute and then you will require a watchman. You will require the protection that the Railway Commission may deem proper to give and then you will insist upon a watchman being added to that.

I purposely evaded that question altogether until the question of ' or ' and ' and ' was settled. Unless we

substitute the word ' and ' for the 'word ' or ' we will not get that protection that the hon. minister describes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend. My hon. friend's argument is that if notwithstanding that the board orders protection to be placed at a crossing an accident happens because of non-compliance with that order no liability results. I cannot agree with that. If the board orders proper protection to be placed at a railway crossing, and the company does not comply with the order of the board and as a result an accident occurs, clearly the company is liable for the damages which may result.
Would the hon. gentleman have any objection substituting the word ' and ' for ' or'?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think it is necessary.
Mr. LANCASTER, it ?
Is there any harm in

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have had this up before. We have discussed it at some length in the House. The hon. gentleman is quite right to push the matter as strenuously as he pleases. I cannot do any more than state my views in the committee. The matter was discussed and discussed before the Railway Committee and now he is back here again. I have expressed my view and I cannot change my mind about that The liability of the company is perfectly clear. McKay vs. the Grand Trunk Railway Company was not decided upon this statute. It was decided upon the previous statute. It was a ease decided by a majority of the Supreme Court reversing the decision of the Court of Appeal of Ontario.

Apart from the words ' or ' or ' and ' I think there is a larger question as to whether the people of the village or town should be compelled to go before the Railway Commission to get an order compelling the railway company to do what the railway company should do and what there should be a statute to compel the rail-v ay company to do. It seems to me that the only objection that there could possibly be to this amendment is that the speed of ten miles an hour is too great. There is too great a danger to human lives occasioned by railway trains running through towns and villages or through districts which are thickly settled at ten miles an hour. In the town in which I live, in which there are 2,000 people and which the Intercolonial Railway runs through, there are neither gates nor watchmen. There is great danger to life, and people have been killed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This would not help my hon. friend.

No, I am only giving this as an illustration. What is true of that town is true of other towns that are crossed by railways. I will take advantage of this occasion to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Em-merson) to the fact that in the town of Sussex there is no protection. I have seen the English mail go through at the rate of sixty miles an hour.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The English mail ?
The train coming from Halifax ; rushing across the main streets of the town at a tremendous rate of speed. The thing is entirely wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is always on Sunday when the people are at church and no one around the streets.

It is only a short time ago that in a neighbouring town two persons who were driving home from church were killed at a crossing. What applies to Sussex, applies to other towns. I fail to see why this provision should not be made statutory, so that it would not be necessary for these small towns and villages to go to the expense and trouble of appearing-before the Railway Commission.

The difficulty from my standpoint is that under the law as declared by the Supreme Court of Canada, if a railway company has its tracks properly fenced along the lands of adjacent proprietors, the trains can run at any speed over highway level crossings. Perhaps an amendment like this would meet the difficulty, and I suggest it to the Minister of Justice :
But unless the board otherwise orders, the speed at any rail level crossing of a highway in a city or town, or in a thickly peopled portion of an incorporated village, shall not exceed ten miles an hour.
Where there are level crossings there should be restriction on the speed of trains, but according to the decision of the Supreme Court there is practically no restriction. The Minister ot Justice doubts as to the correctness of that decision, but until it is over-rilled by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, or until its effect is taken away by legislation, it will remain the law of the land. There appears to be no limit at all to the speed at which trains may pass over a level highway crossing so long as the bell is rung, and so long as the lands of adjacent proprietors are properly fenced. The fencing of the lands does not help the situation at the crossings, and when a train is running twentv or thirty miles an hour, the ringing of the' bell may not be sufficient protection. Some ten or twelve years ago, a very respected old gentleman, a prominent citizen of my pro-

vince, whose hearing was somewhat impaired, was instantly killed at one of these crossings by a train running at a very excessive rate of speed. In countries which are more advanced than ours, level crossings are not permitted. It is most unusual to find them in Great Britain. In all my travels there I have only seen one or two, and then in the most remote parts of the country.
And they are protected by gates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They are very common in the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are. If we have to permit them here in Canada it does seem to me proper that there should be some restriction upon the speed at which trains shall run over these level crossings.

Representing, .as I do, the locality in which one of these accidents occurred, I certainly believe that in justice to the residents there some arrangement should be made to place a watchman and gates at that crossing. I sincerely hope that the Railway Commissioners will take that matter into their serious consideration. The people who were killed in the accident referred to, were driving home from the fall fair ; the train was going at a much faster rate than usual, and they were unable to get out of the way. The Ontario courts awarded damages and in the Supreme Court, while one judge upheld the decision of the lower courts, three judges were against it and it was reversed. These people have been put to a great deal of expenses in endeavouring to obtain justice, and in order to prevent such accidents in future, we should legislate here that there should be more protection at these crossings.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The promoter of this Bill has perhaps unintentionally, but at all events very unfairly reflected upon the attitude of the committee. The committee gave this Bill fair consideration, and there was no disrespect shown to the Bill, or its promoter. The law now reads :
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act ; or, unless permission is given by some regulation or order of the hoard. The board may change such speed in any case to any rate which it deems expedient.
If the law were amended as proposed, it would read :
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village, at a speed greater than ten njiles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected in the
manner prescribed by this Act, or unless permission is given by some regulation or order of the board. The board may change such speed in any case to any rate which it deems expedient ; and wherever in any city, town or incorporated village any railway crosses on the highway at rail level, the said speed of ten miles an hour shall in no event be exceeded unless the railway company keeps a watchman at said crossing to warn all persons using the highway of approaching trains.
This matter was considered by the Railway Committee from the standpoint of the Railway Act of last session which has only been in operation for a year, and which made provision for protecting crossings throughout the country. For this parliament to pass an arbitrary enactment such as is proposed by this Bill would create a hardship and would involve no greater protection
In view of the decision of the Supreme Court on the construction of the word ' fencing,' will the hon. gentleman say that the present law is effective ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will deal with that in a moment. I was saying that the railway company dealt with this Bill from the standpoint of the Railway Act of last session which made proper provision for restricting the speed of trains in towns and villages. Now he proposes an amendment which, if carried into effect, would mean that If there were a watchman there, no matter how thickly peopled or well settled it might be, a train could go through that town or city at an unlimited speed. The very case which has been cited arose out of an accident that occurred because of the negligence of a watchman. The presence of a watchman is not at all times a safeguard against accidents. There will be accidents although there are watchmen. It is so along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. We have patent semaphores and also watchmen at important crossings ; yet accidents occur and people are injured and sometimes killed. But this abitrary enactment which does not provide for adequate safeguards in thickly-settled sections, Is to my mind objectionable legislation. Moreover it requires a watchman at every crossing in every town anil village in every section of the country. My hon. friend lias referred to the town in which he lives. Take an illustration from another section in his vicinity. There is a railway running from Havelock In the county of King's, N.B., to Elgin In the county of Albert. It runs from one point to another in the morning, and returns in the evening. I do not know that it is ever guilty of speed exceeding ten miles an hour ; but the Bill of my hon. friend would require that railway to have a watchman at every crossing in the villages through which it passes.
If it exceeds ten miles [DOT] an hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It does sometimes exceed ten miles an hour. It cannot have a watchman on tap, for special occasions; but it must have a watchman at each crossing during the whole season.
I would remind my hon. friend that those villages are not incorporated, and therefore do not come uuder the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Some of them are. Take the town of Sackville, which is an incorporated town. The town from which my hon. friend comes has within the last few weeks, I believe, been raised to the dignity of an incorporated town. It would be absurd to say that all crossings are dangerous. It is within the knowledge of hon. gentlemen opposite that at many crossings, even in incorporated towns, there is no possible danger, while at other crossings in the same towns it would be necessary to have protections. Where the view is obscured it is very necessary that there should be protection sometimes even in addition to a watchman. It seems to me, therefore, that it woluld be entirely arbitrary to have a provision such as this, requiring that at all level crossings, within the limits of every incorporated town and village, watchmen should be placed.

Would the hon. Minister of Railways agree to the Bill if I inserted in it the words ' thickly-peopled ' ? Let us see what we are fighting. I understand the hon. Minister to argue that if a place were thickly-peopled, or the buildings were constructed close to each other, so that the view would be obscured, it would be necessary to have this protection. I have drawn this provision on the assumption that the view is generally obstructed in an incorporated town or village. If the hon. Minister of Railways can find an odd crossing here or there where the view is not obstructed as much as at others, it does not follow, because of that unique and exceptional instance, that the railways should be allowed to go on killing people. The hon. gentleman is evidently not keeping pace with the times with regard to the number of accidents that happen. You can hardly take up a newspaper without reading an account of a man being killed at a railway crossing. Railway people may say that he was careless or was guilty of contributory negligence ; but that statement does not prevent the accidents occurring. If the minister thinks my Bill too drastic, and is content to have it with the words ' thickly-peopled ' inserted in it. I am willing to make that amendment.
