This parliament has solemnly declared that there should be some protection for people in the thickly-settled portions of cities, towns and villages. That Act has been in force since 1888, and last year parliament declared that there should be some special protection provided. If some such amendment as mine is not

made, that whole section should be repealed, because it has no effect; it does not accomplish anything The hon. gentleman says, you can get protection by obtaining a special order from the Railway Commission. If that is so, there is no need of this section. Why do the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways not unite to strike out that whole section. What does it mean ? It has always been proposed to provide some general protection to the people in the thickly-peopled portions of cities, towns and villages. I admit that I have gone a little farther by-declaring that every crossing in a city, town or village is in a thickly-settled district. If I cannot get that much, let us at any rate do something to save some of these lives.
Let us put in the words ' thickly peopled ' and then we will be consistent with the Act as it is now. The Act surely means something. It says that trains are not to exceed 10 miles an hour when passing through any jthickly peopled portion of any city, town or vilage. That has been the law since 1888, and last year it was unanimously reenacted by this House. What does parliament intend by that ? What evil are they trying to remedy, what danger are they trying to avert ? Surely it is the danger of trains going at a fast rate over the level crossings described in the Act. The object of the section is surely that people who approach a crossing in a town or village shall have a right to expect that trains will not pass over it at a rate in excess of 10 miles an hour according to the legislation of last year, or 6 miles an hour according to the law as it was prior to that time. With this section in force people will of course conclude that a train has no right to run at that rate, uhless there is some protection at the crossing, and seeing a train approaching at a more rapid rate they naturally conclude that there is a portection and so possibly drive on to death or injury and in doing so,
I do not believe they are guilty of recklessness. I appeal to the Minister of Railways; he seems to be trying to do what I am, but he does not agree with my method. Let us see if I cannot agree with his. He suggests that we should put in ' where the view is obstructed watchmen' or something should be ordered if trains are going 50 miles an hour as they are going every day in my part of the country, some protection should certainly be provided. If the hon. minister had been in Grimsby a little over a year ago, he might have seen the public funeral of three young people, who while going home from church were killed at a level crossing by a train going at the rate of 50 ;miles an hour. |The train does not stop between St. Catharines and Hamilton and I am sure if the minister had witnessed that funeral he would have thought that some law was necessary. Our object is not to make railways liable for damages for accidents that may occur

but to prevent accidents happening. The railways will not make any effort to prevent accidents or to do anything but make money out of the people, and to make fast travel unless they are compelled to do so. The Minister of Kailways seems to agree that where the view is obstructed watchmen would be necessary. Then what is the harm in saying that a watchman is necessary and why should we have to go through the form of multiplying the work of the Railway Commission and having an order issued in each specific case ? We have a declaration in the law now, even if my amendment is thrown out, that trains are not to exceed 10 miles an hour in thickly peopled portions of cities, towns and villages. Surely if they do that some one should be responsible for any damage that may be caused by such excess, or liable to punishment for breach of that law. The minister thinks that where the view is obstructed and the place thickly peopled there should be a watchman. Let the Minister of Railways help me no matter if I am a member of the opposition. We are all Canadians and want to save Canadian lives. Let him help me to construct a statute according to my view. Let him put ' thickly peopled ' and ' where the view is obstructed,' and leave it to a court to find the fact. Let him make such an amendment to the Railway Act and it will do more to make him popular as Minister of Railways than anything he has done. It must be i-emembered that all cities, towns and vilages are thickly peopled. Villages are not incorporated until they are thickly peopled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my bon. friend think he has omitted the words ' thickly peopled ? '
The words 'thickly peopled ' are not in my amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Read it.

The statute says :
No train shall pass in or through any thickly peopled portion of any city, town or village at a rate exceeding ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected.
And so on. And I add :
And wherever in a city, town or incorporated village a railway crosses a highway at rail-level, the said speed of ten miles an hour shall in no event he exceeded, unless the railway company keeps a watchman at such crossing to warn all persons using the highway of approaching trains.
I drew the amendment and I thought I knew what was, in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I adhere to what I said ; I have the Bill before me. Why do the words ' thickly peopled ' in the first part of the section not apply to this ?
I said not five minutes ago that the words were in the original law but not in mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are in the
section you are amending.
Mr. LANCASTER, My hon. friend might be serious ; some of us are serious. The Minister of Justice need not think that by quibbling he will knock me off my feet, because I have been in as much trouble as 1 am now, and have got out of it. I want to treat things seriously and I want them treated seriously. I stated that the words ' thickly peopled ' were in the original law, and he objects, because I do not limit it by putting in the words ' thickly peopled portion ' in my amendment ? But this Bill provides that in cities, towns and villages, watchmen shall be provided at rail level crossings where the speed of ten miles an hour is exceeded. The Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways find fault with the exact construction of the sentences in this Bill, but they tacitly admit that the object is to avoid the destruction of life at these crossings, and that we do not want the rate of ten miles an hour to be exceeded without some one being liable. If the Minister of Justice thinks that because the railways will be bound to do one thing or the other that, therefore, they will be bound to do both, he cannot regard it as of any disadvantage to put in the word ' and' instead of the word ' or, ' and then the language of the section will be what we both think it ought to be. If the Minister of Railways thinks that I am calling for watchmen to be stationed where they are not necessary, I am willing to insert tne words ' thickly peopled portion of ' before ' cities, towns or incorporated villages. ' I am willing to accept what I can get, if I cannot get all I want. Let .us save as many lives as we can. I am willing, if the Minister of Railways desires it. to insert ' where the view is obstructed. ' Those are his words, and I suppose he used them advisedly. If he desires the Bill to be amended in this way, I suppose he thinks that the principle of the Bill will prevail. It is because the view is obstructed in all cities, towns and incorporated villages that this amendment is necessary. In every thickly peopled place the view is obstructed by buildings and the hearing is obstructed by the noises of the city, town or village. Let me tell the Minister of Justice that people who are injured at railway crossings, or the representatives of those who are killed do not wish to come down here to the Supreme Court to have an argument by eminent counsel as to the construction of the word ' or ' and the word ' and, ' in order to ascertain whether the member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) was right when he said that ' or ' meant or, or whether the Minister of Justice was right when he said that the word ' or ' meant and.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say so.

Then, if it does not mean ' and, ' we are not giving tlie protection that the Minister of Justice said we are giving. What is the use of having anything in the law with regard to the protection of crossings at rail level if the railway company can plead : It is true we have not protected the crossing as the law required, but we have fenced the right of way up to the highway and turned the fence into the cattle-guard, and the Supreme Court has decided that that is ail that we have to do- we are bound to fence or to protect, bound to do one or the other-and, so long as we do either, we can kill as many people as we like at these crossings ? The law provides that the railway shall run at a slower rate of speed at these crossings than elsewhere. But under the decision of the Supreme Court, in effect, that section does not mean anything ; it does not accomplish anything. Because I think the Minister of Justice will agree that, according to his own argument, they are bound to fence, under certain sections, and they are bound to protect under certain other sections, if an order of the Railway Commission is given directing them to do so. What can be the meaning of this section if it is not that at these particular points, these level crossings, they are not to run as fast as at other places ? Because it is at these points that the danger is, a danger to which ail classes of the community is exposed ; the farmer going to market, the labourer going to work, the child going to school, all classes going to or coming from church-for it was in returning from church one evening after dark that these people of whom I have spoken were killed at the crossing at Grimsby. Now, there is another point that I have not yet mentioned and that nobody else, so far as I know has said anything about. And, when I state it, some hon. members on the other side who are now laughing, as if this were all a joke, may think that there is something in it. Suppose that a farmer is accustomed to enter a city by a certain road on which there is a level crossing with a watchman to warn people of the approach of trains. Is it not the most reasonable thing in the world to believe even if he changes his route and crosses the railway at another street, he will, unthinkingly depend upon being warned if the train is approaching ? And it is not reasonable that we should make some general rule upon which the people can depend, and not compel a man, when he approaches a level crossing in a city, town or village, to try to recall to his memory whether this is one of the crossings for which the railway commission has ordered protection, or whether it is one where the public cross entirely at their own risk ? But that is what this statute will mean if you do not make some law that applies to all cities, towns and incorporated villages. Is there an hon. gentleman here who does not' believe that it

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
would be safer to guard every highway crossing in a city, town or village, so that people might know exactly what' they\ have to rely upon ? Of course, in the open country, there is not the same need, because, the place not being ' thickly populated, ' there are no buildings to obstruct the view and no noises to interfere with one hearing approaching trains. Why should there be a watchman, for instance, at Depot street, in Grimsby, and no watchman at Elizabeth street a hundred yards away and at a point as thickly populated as the other if they were both on the level of the highway? Surely the simplest, most eflieient way would have been to have one rule which would apply easily to all places under similar conditions. It is true, that watchmen will cost the railway company something. That was the whole contention of the counsel that appeared before the Railway Committee-that this amendment would cost them money. But they get the use of the highway for nothing, and it seems to me only reasonable that they should expect to pay some toll in order to provide means to prevent people from being killed who wish to use the highway.
While it is going to cost them money to do it, it will not cost people their lives. They say it will cost them $2.70 at each crossing during the twenty-four hours, and they multiply that by all the level crossings in the country, and say that it would cost them a million or a million and a half of money, and therefore we should not impose this costly legislation upon them. But in the same breath the counsel for the railways argued that there was no need of this law, because they were going to convert all their level crossings into overhead or underground crossings. Yet they did not seem to see that the moment they converted the level crossing into an underground or overhead crossing my law would not apply to them. That is the sort of argument you get from railway counsel arguing before the Railway Committee why a public Bill should not pass. They say : We are going to convert all our level crossings as fast as we can into crossings that are not on the level ; and in the same breath they say it will cost them so much money to keep watchmen at each of these level crossings, and therefore we ought not to impose that burden upon them. Now, they cannot find fault with us if we accept their own statement. As soon as they convert their crossings they can take away their watchmen. In the older parts of the empire, around London, England, where I was born, you did not find a level crossing unless there was a watchman with a flag.
But you are a foreigner.

I may be, in the premier's opinion, but as long as I am a 1 member of this House of Commons I

am going to speak in favour of the people who sent me here. In England these watchmen are either one-armed or one-legged, as a rule, because when a railway employee gets maimed the companies make him a watchman at a crossing-pension him in this way ; and so he saves life while he is there, and makes a living, and at the same time the railways become popular with the people, because they do- not kill them. Now, this parliament might teach the railways of this country something by adopting this legislation ; we could teach them that although they are not bound at present, and would not necessarily be bound if this Act were passed, to employ men as watchman that they happen to have maimed, still if they choose to pension their men in that way they could -well do it, and at the same time preserve the lives of the people crossing their railways and avoiding accidents for damages. Now, I want to impress upon the Minister of Railways what I said before I sit down. It may be that I am not advocating this measure irsthe best manner, it is possible that in my earnestness, and in my desire to accomplish what I think is right, I am not arguing my cause with the suavity possessed by the 'Minister of Justice or the Minister of Railways. This is not a party question, and I hope that the protection of the people's lives will never become a party question in this country ; therefore, I ask the ministers and the House to consider a little further what I have said about this measure ; to ask themselves whether, after having put in the words ' thickly peopled and where the view is obstructed,' they have done any harm by this legislation ? as it now' stands, the legislation is not practical. To say that a railway train must not exceed ten miles an hour in a certain place and yet to say at the same time that thejr are not liable if they do exceed that rate unle'ss they have got an order from some authority to say that they shall not exceed it unless on certain conditions-that is round-about legislation, and it will give rise to losses and cause trouble. We have here in my amendment a clear declaration that in certain places that are thickly peopled, and where the view is obstructed, they are bound to have a w'atchman to warn the people of approaching trains, otherwise they cannot exceed ten miles an hour. Then there w'ill he no question that if they want to run their trains faster than ten miles an hour they must employ watchmen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is only one difficulty that I see with this amendment, and it is a serious one. Would the hon. member say what w'ould he the proper protection required by the Act supposing we substituted ' and 'for ' or ' ?
Six o'clock.

I will answer the question after recess.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
.Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. LANCASTER, jir. Speaker, w'hen the- committee rose at six o'clock my hon. friend the Minister of Justice asked me if I would tell him at eight o'clock what the effect of my amendment w'ould be. As I understood him, he wanted me to say what protection -would be the result of my amendment. My answer is that the effect of my amendment that at all these crossings on the rail level where trains exceed ten miles an hour w'ithin the limits of cities, towns and incorporated villages, there will he a watchman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What I wanted to know was if you substituted ' and ' for ' or ' what -would ' properly protected ' mean ?
Without any other amendment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No other amendment.

The effect would he that the only protection that there would be at these crossings would he such protection as is ordered by the Railway Commission under some of those different sections which the hon. Minister of Justice referred to this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You would not be any further ahead.

We would be this much farther ahead, that if we did go to the trouble to get an order from the Railway Commission it would have to be carried out, and if the railway company did not protect under that order and under the requirements with the words ' and ' inserted in the section, they would be liable. If we do not have the word ' and ' in the Act and we get an order from the Railway Commission the railway company would be in a position to say we are not bound both to fence -and protect, because we are only bound to fence or protect. We have our fences up to the highway and turned into the cattle-guards, so that we are not liable under the circumstances. With my whole amendment there would be more protection, the railway company would be obliged to protect by a watchman at all those crossings on the rail level where their trains exceeded ten miles an hour within the limits of cities, towns and incorporated villages and in addition they would be obliged to furnish such other protection as in any special case an application was made to and an order granted by the Railway Commission. My law would not affect them at all unless they exceeded ten miles an hour. The Railway Commission have it in their power to keep their trains1 down in these places under ten miles an hour or

else to put on a watchman if my amendment carries.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), was good enough to say that we all desired the same thing, that is to lessen the danger in respect to level railway crossings. I think we all 'have that object in view. It is only a difference as to the methods to be pursued. It seems to me that the proposed amendment of my hon. friend is objectionable from two or three standpoints. I have already explained briefly in what way, but I would give a farther reason, and it is that it would limit the discretion and power of the Railway Commission. If there is a dangerous crossing, whether it is within the limits of any city, incorporated town, or village, or whether it is through the country generally and it is brought to their notice they have the power to order in respect to that particular crossing the railway company to afford all the protection that may be necessary.
Can they not do so if my amendment is passed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Your amendment limits the discretion and power and it is inconsistent with the previous provision in the same; section giving the board permission to allow an increase in the rate of speed. I have pointed out already that if this arbitrary enactment were to be acknowledged by this committee under such circumstances there would be no limitation to the speed of the train within the limits of any corporation if a watchman were provided. That would be inadequate. The mere fact of having a watchman would not be a protection to the public, and yet it would be a protection to the railway company. If they had a watchman they could put their trains through the bounds of the corporation at any speed they chose. I think that will be acknowledged by my hon. friend.
No, nq, not at all. That is- not the result, in my opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: According to his proposal it is made to apply whether a portion of the city, town or incorporated village is thickly peopled or not.
Suppose we insert the words ' thickly peopled.' That would do away with that objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not think that would carry it any further according to the argument of my hon.- friend. There are many level crossings throughout Canada which do not require a watchman to protect them. Admittedly they do not require a watcnman, but yet the enactment of my hon. friend would demand that there should be a watchman there. Under his amendment there would be the privilege of un-Mr. LANCASTER.
limited speed given to the railway companies, and I think the provisions of the Railway Act, as contained in section 25, afford all the protection that the public require in the case of dangerous crossings whether within the limits of incorporated towns, or villages, or cities, or whether outside of the bounds. The Railway Commission, under subsection (a) of section 25 of the Railway Act, have power to make orders and regulations :
Limiting the rate of speed at which railway trains and locomotives may he run in any city, town or village, or in any class of cities, towns or villages described in any regulation ; and, if the board thinks fit, the rate of speed within certain described portions of any city, town or village, and allowing another rate of speed in other portions thereof.
It seems to me that this is the only sensible way to regulate these matters. You would have, by the proposed enactment, an arbitrary cast iron rule to apply to the whole country. It would be unfair to apply it to the whole country, it would be adding unnecesssary expense and especially in this country where we must recognize conditions and where we must have regard to sparsely settled communities. There are in this country incorporated villages where there are only BOO inhabitants. Will any one say that unless there is some crossing within the limits of that corporation which is dangerous there should necessarily he a watchman any more than there should be a watchman In some of the country districts which are not incorporated. But in that case if there were a dangerous crossing within the municipal limits you could apply to the Railway Commission, and you could have whatever regulation the judgment of the commission would deem it necessary to pass. The same is true in respect to ' any crossing throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion. The Railway Commission is clothed with full powers to require whatever protection they may think necessary. It does seem to me unwise that within a few months after the Railway Commission has come into being, and without our having any experience of the working of the new railway Act, we should now proceed to make amendments. It is not desirable to Interfere with tlie existing law unless cogent reasons are shown for such interference. If this amendment should pass we would take away from the Railway Commission the powers we have given it.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Most decidedly you do.
The Railway Commission have the right to regulate the speed, but what is the sense of section 227 as it now stands ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This amendment to the Act is objectionable for the reason that

it restricts the power and discretion of the railway board, under which they can increase, or decrease, the rate of speed as they may deem expedient. If this clause is tacked on to the section it certainly limits the power of the railway board.
Has the Railway Commission power to limit the rate of speed to less than ten miles an hour ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Under the existing Act the Railway Commission has full power to order trains to run at less than ten miles an hour. It seems to me that my hon. friend has not shown good cause for his amendment. As it is now, and as I think it ought to be, each crossing must stand on its own merits and be considered individually ; from the use made of it; the population in the vicinity, and its danger generally. In legislating here we cannot know the conditions which prevail at the different crossings throughout Canada, and no cast iron rule can apply to all, bec'ause what may be desirable in one place might be very undesirable in another. We must recognize that the public interest demands that fast trains must be run If we are to keep pace with the times there must be fast express trains and we cannot have fast express trains unless under certain conditions they have the right to go at speed on rail level crossings. If in the exercise of that right there is danger to the public at any particular highway crossing then the Board of Railway Commissioners have the power to take it into consideration and provide a remedy. Accidents often do happen and we all deplore them, but very often these accidents are not due to trains running at speed. The fact that trains do run at speed is only one cause of accident, a cause we should guard against it is true, but still it is only one cause and we must not forget that these accidents are often due to other reasons.
While it is a disease for which a remedy should be applied, it is not the only disease. Therefore it seems to me that the commission can better have regard to all the causes than this parliament can have regard to only one cause, that is, the cause of speed. I mentioned incidentally that there are many crossings which are dangerous solely because of the view being obscured. It does not make much difference whether a train runs at a very great speed or at a lesser speed. There is a difference in degree, I admit, but the_danger is there just the same, and you cannot remove that danger by merely providing against extreme speed. By application to the commission, and by placing all the facts before them, you can have a remedy applied which is to the point, which is suitable to that particular crossing, and which affords protection. I think my hon. friend places too much reliance upon a watchman. I know from my own experience that in too many eases that is not a protection against loss to life and limb. I prefer rather to leave the wbrking
out of this difficulty to the Railway Commission, as provided by the Act passed last year.
I think this is too early a stage for us to attempt to pass any amendments to that Act. Its operation is the test, and if after its operation for a time, the remedy of the Railway Commission is found to be inadequate, it will be time for this parliament to provide other remedies. But at present it seems to me that no good cause has been shown why we should make this change, and remove from the commission the powers which we have given them in this regard ; because I hold that we would be removing from them, in degree at least, their powers, and would be limiting their right of action for good.
Can the hon. minister state to the committee any serious accident that has taken place at any crossing where a watchman was provided ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, a great fnany. The very case cited by my hon. friend-one of the cases before the courts of Ontario- was a case in which there was loss of life, I think, although there was a watchman. The fact of a watchman being there is no absolute safeguard. I grant that it .is some measure of protection. But if the Bill became law, the mere fact that the railway company had provided a watchman would of itself be a rebuttal of any negligence on their part, and there would be no remedy against them. Moreover, it would enable the railway company, notwithstanding the provisions of section 227, to run its trains at any speed, whereas under the provisions of the section at present there is a limitation as to speed.

I am sorry that the Minister of Railways has said that it is not necessary to consider the section of the Act I am proposing to amend. It is almost impossible to convince any hon. gentlemen who makes that statement that an amendment is right. I have never before heard it suggested that it was not necessary to consider the document you are proposing to amend. The hon. gentleman persists in referring to the provisions of the Act giving the Railway Commission power to regulate speed and other matters entirely outside of the section before the committee ; and I suppose it is almost hopeless to expect the section I am seeking to amend to be properly understood by the committee if there are many hon. gentlemen like the Minister of Railways who believes it is not necessary to consider that section. The hon. minister took very good care not to attempt to explain the section. He does not say, in answer to me, what the object of the section is ; but he says that no good could come of the amendment which I wish to make to that section.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I say it would make it worse.

The hon. gentleman ought to have been able to tell us ivhat the object of the section as it stands is. That section in substance has been in the law since 1888. It provides that no train shall pass through a thickly-settled portion of any city, town or village at a speed greater than ten miles an hour-it used to be six miles. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council had power to make regulations with regard to railways crossings, and the hon. gentlemen will have the commission deal with that same matter as if this section did not exist at all. If the hon. gentleman's argument amounts to anything, it amounts to this, that because you can get a special provision from the Railway Commission, you do not need anything else. If that is the case, this section should be struck out of the statute altogether. I am inclined to believe that the Minister of Railways does not understand that section, or does not bother his head about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Pardon me : I read the section.	.

That section contains a declaration of this parliament that no train shall pass at a speed greater than ten miles an hour. We know that other parts of the Act provide that the Railway Commission can regulate the speed at any rate they deem expedient. The hon. gentleman says that if we pass this Bill, we override tlie powers of the Railway Commission. Now, I propose to show that in that the hon. minister is entirely wrong. As the section stands unamended, it is inconsistent, while my proposed amendment clears it up. As it stands, it is simply an invitation to have lawsuits. One lawyer will say that you must take the whole section and that reading it altogether the meaning is that the speed shall not exceed ten miles an hour, but the board may say that it shall not exceed twelve or fifteen miles. Another lawyer will say that the board can regulate the speed in any fashion and that seems to be the construction put upon it by the minister, that they can regulate it to five or six miles, notwithstanding the statute says it shall not exceed ten miles. My amendment removes all ambiguities and says that in no case shall the speed exceed ten miles unless they have a watchman.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman in his amendment says :
And wherever in a city, town or incorporated village a railway crosses a highway at rail-level, the said speed of ten miles an hour shall in no event he exceeded, unless the railway company keeps a watchman at such crossing to warn ail persons using the highway of approaching trains.
That might be in the suburbs of a town where there are no inhabitants. ' Wherever in a town, city, or village ' ; there might Mr. EMMERSON.
be no necessity for it in the outskirts. The section as it now stands says that no train shall pass through any thickly peopled portion at high speed, hut the proposed amendment would require a watchman at every crossing in the approaches to a city, even in districts where there might be no inhabitants, and yet the train would bo required to slow up at each of these crossings.
That was not the point I was discussing when the minister interrupted me. However, if he wishes to discuss that I will go back to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I wish the hon. gentleman to discuss it and therefore I called his attention to it.

Before six o'clock I pointed out half a dozen times ; it was necessary to do so because the minister did not seem to understand, that if he wants to insert the words ' thickly peopled ' in my amendment, I am willing to accept that. I have said that at least six times, and I hope the hon. gentleman will not again bring that up as a supposed answer to something I am discussing. I was saying that the power of the board for which he contends, is not interfered with in that section. By my section it is made clear that if they exceed ten miles an hour, they must at least have a watchman^ and if they have a watchman, they can go as fast as they like if the board permits them to do so. There is not the least excuse for the argument that this limits the power or discretion of the commission. It does carry out what the section says in the beginning. In that is contained the declaration of the policy or the intention of the legislature of this country that as a rule the speed of trains in these thickly peopled portions is not to he more than ten miles an hour, where there is no protection in cities, towns and villages. When you come on with an amendment to legislate out the decision of the Supreme Court which has made this section nugatory, you are doing something in the interest of the whole country, not only by the protection of life, but also by making the law certain and clear. To say that It is interfering with the powers of the board to provide that the rate is not to exceed ten miles an hour, is unreasonable.
How can the minister contend that my amendment is inconsistent with the intention of the section and at the same time not move in amendment to strike out the whole of section 227 is what I cannot understand, because if his argument amounts to anything this section 227 does not accomplish anything and should not be in the statute. He does not pretend to say what it does accomplish, but claims that the law is sufficient without section 227 at all. The hon. gentleman says that this is an arbitrary

enactment, and it would not be possible, if this section passed, to more closely limit the speed of any trains. If that argument was good, it must be based upon the idea that this enactment will repeal all the other sections giving power to the commission to regulate the speed of trains. As a matter of fact this section does not say a word about that, but it only provides that either the speed provided for must not be exceeded or else a watchman must be provided. I am not saying that the speed should be left at ten miles an hour, but I am only carrying into effect the law as it stands. The only object is to ask parliament to enact that this provision of the law shall mean something and be practical and effective. The hon. gentleman says there are a number of crossings that do not require watchmen. If he means that there are crossings in the thickly peopled portions of cities, towns and villages that they do not require watchmen I will not waste the time of the committee in answering him. I leave that to the judgment of members of this committee. I cannot suppose that that is just what the hon. gentleman meant. I assume that what he meant was that there are crossings which do not require watchmen, that they can be better protected in some other way than by watchmen. If so, he is assuming the very contrary of what the statute has required ever since 1888. But the hon. gentleman is careful not to say what protection is better than watchmen. He tells us that the member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is not right, but I am going to ask the committee to assume that my suggestion is a good one when the hon. gentleman himself does not offer a better. Minister of Railways, though he be, he has no right to ask this committee to refuse to accept a proposed remedy when he himself has nothing else to propose. But, let me tell him why the watchman is the best way of providing protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: How about gates?
If you have gates you must have some one there to watch them and to operate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Why not automatic gates ?

I understand the minister to say that some one can be employed to operate them. The Railway Commission may order gates as well as watchmen. I shall not complain, because the public will be all the better protected. But if you have only the one means of protection, the watchman is the best. If you have gates and no one to operate them but the person who wishes to cross you have the gates raised by people who know nothing about the times -when trains may be expected. But a watchman employed by the railway may be supposed to know when trains are to be expected-it is his business to know, and
we must assume that men will do their duty. Then, a watchman is not inanimate, he is not a fixture. If he sees a person crossing he can call to him, if necessary he can follow him and make sure that his warning is heard. He can continue his warnings until he accomplishes his purpose, which is to prevent the impact of the swiftly moving train upon the human body.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) mean to say that there are no automatic gates that can be used without watchmen ?

I do not say that; but the hon. gentleman will find that the railways would prefer to provide watchmen rather than these automatic gates, as being less expensive. This Bill will not apply to every crossing, because there are many of them in cities, towns and villages in which the railway runs either over or under the highway and in such cases they would not apply. Though the Minister of Railways has not ventured to make a suggestion himself I will complete what I was saying of the advantages of watchmen over other means of protection. The hon. minister told my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Bain) that there was a watchman at the crossings at which the McKay case arose. But, let me tell the hon. gentleman, the railway company had no watchman there. The village of Forest, knowing that this was a dangerous crossing provided a watchman for this particular day, which was fair day, and they knew that there was special danger of accident on that day. But this watchman knew- nothing about the hours of trains. And I suppose that he felt that his responsibility was not very great, because he was not employed by the railway and the railway could not discipline him even if a dozen people were killed. The jury found that the train that killed Mrs. McKay and the children was going at an excessive rate of speed, and when Mr. McKay sued he was awarded damages. The rate of speed was twenty miles an hour, and the jury thought, as parliament has thought every since 1888, that that was an excessive rate of speed for the thickly peopled portion of a city, town or village. It was 14 miles an hour faster than the statute then said it should be, which was 6 miles an hour. The jury agreed with this parliament, which called it 6 miles an hour. There was no protection there by law. They had their tracks fenced, the fences turned into the highways, but that is no protection to the traveller. The Court of Appeal of Ontario sustained that judgment, and the Supreme Court judges by a majority declared the law to be of such a nature that it is necessary for the statute to be amended in this House. The Supreme Court expected the Minister of Railways to say: In view of that state of the law we must override that decision by an amendment. The judges stated that the fencing required by the Act was

only to reach up to the highway, turning into the cattle-guards. It is all very well to say that people should be protected here, but it is no good to say that, unless some hon. gentlemen suggest a way of protection. To say that the Railway Commission in each case can make an order as they think necessary is no answer unless we are going to say that this section should not be in the statutes at all, that parliament should not make a declaration that the greatest speed should not exceed 10 miles an hour. Formerly it was 6 miles an hour, and Mr. Blau thought 6 miles an hour was a little too slow to make them run, but he did not strike out the section and left it at 10 miles. Now is this parliament going to allow a section lo be declared nugatory by the Supreme Court without amending it, or without having the courage to strike out the whole section ? I am bound to point out to the Minister of Railways that if he rejects my amendment and does not put in another to make this section practical, he is coolly insisting on a section remaining in the statute that the Supreme Court of Canada says is of no effect.
Now the Minister of Railways referred to section 25 of the Railway Act as to the power of the board. I cannot see why he made that reference. That is a general section giving power to the board to make regulations limiting the rate of speed, specifying the means of protection and so forth, stating in general terms what the powers of tlie Railway Commission should be in every matter. That section. simply gives them jurisdiction in general terms over the speed 'of trains and these other matters, but it does not have any effect to make my amendment inconsistent. But that section 2o must be read in the light of section 227 and means that, subject to 227, which fixes the rate of speed in cities, towns and villages at 10 miles an hour, the board is to have jurisdiction in all other respects. I thought the minister was going to help the House to do something practical but he has not. Now again, I ask the minister what is the object of section 227 ? Here is a parliament solemnly declaring every year in a general law that no rate of speed should be exceeded, that a certain rate which was formerly 6 miles an hour and now 10, shall not be exceeded in those places ; and yet, without repealing this section the minister would suggest that I add to it * whenever the board does not allow that rate to be exceeded.' What would the section mean then ? It would state in one place that no train shall go faster than 10 miles an hour at those places, but at the same time the board can allow it to go faster if it chooses. I submit, Mr, Chairman, that instead of the minister saying that I have made out no case, there is no excuse for him opposing this amendment. To say that we had better wait until we see what the
Railway Commission will do, does not help us at all if the law is wrong. Why should we wait to see whether the Railway Commission will be able to accomplish something that on the face of it we cannot expect them to do ? The Railway Commission is not going to regulate this rate of speed at 10 miles an hour. If you reject my amendment and refuse to say that this is the opinion of parliament, the Railway Commission at once, if they know what happens in this House to-night, will say : Parliament does not intend to force railway trains to run at so slow a rate as 10 miles an hour, even if the track is not protected. Take a case where the board would not make any order as to protection would not order a watchman or gates ; at the same time, according to the Minister of Railways, they could allow a train to run in one village at 10 miles and in another at only 6 or 8 miles an hour. Now how is that going to work ?
A man driving along gets accustomed, when he sees a train so far off, to judge how long it will take it to get to the crossing which he is approaching. To say that the rate of speed is not the'cause of these accidents is, in my opinion, not correct. It is the cause of the accident. A man sees a train approaching him at a certain distance, and expecting that the train is moving at the rate of eight or ten miles an hour he knows he can get past it before it comes to the crossing, but if it is going five times as fast as that, or if it is going at the rate of twenty-five miles an hour, he is not prepared' for such a speed, and when he attempts to cross the train strikes him, and he is either killed or injured. If so, it is the fault of this parliament and of this government. To make the law reasonable and fair to the people as well as to the railways, you should have a declaration in it-you have the declaration in it now, but it is so construed by the courts that it cannot be carreid out- that the railway companies must provide watchmen if their trains exceed a rate of ten miles an hour. If the train is going at a faster rate than ten miles an hour a man approaching the crossing is warned and protected by the watchmen. It has been said that the rate of speed does not affect the obstruction of the view, but if the view is obstructed the rate of speed makes a difference, because if the train is going at a rate of speed four or five times as fast as the man travelling along the road thought it was going he will not have time to get out of the way. I cannot understand why the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals does not adopt this amendment, and I submit that the majority of the committee, even if the hon. Minister of Railways does not support it, ought to vote for it so as to make the statute workable for the benefit of the people, because, as I have pointed out, the Supreme Court has decided that it is of no effect at all as it stands to-day.

Knowing, as he does, the ease which took place in Forest, whereby two or three people were killed, I want to ask the hon. Minister of Railways whether he would approve of having a watchman at that point or not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am not familiar with the circumstances of the case to which my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) refers. I can only say to him that the Jaw as it now stands provides a remedy, and that if gates or a watchman are required the Railway Commission has full power to deal with the matter, and it is entirely foreign to the proposition of my hon. friend here to-night The Railway Commission has jurisdiction over the matter. I have not.

I think my hon. friend from Iiincohi (Mr. Lancaster) should get some consideration at the hands of the government in connection with \this important Question. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) has had brought to his attention the very serious accidents that have occurred in different parts of Canada during the last few years. I am not going to enter into a discussion of the old or new law, but 1 am of the opinion that it is the duty of the government at this session of parliament to make the law so plain that all important crossings in the different municipalities should have proper protection, whatever that protection may be. In the county I have the honour to represent there has been very general complaining in this respect for many years. At the last session of parliament this new Act was passed, but notwithstanding there are accidents taking place in different parts of Canada at railway crossings. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals seems to fear lest the Railway Commission's duties should be somewhat crippled, but, if I am correctly informed, since the Railway Commission has been appointed there have been some three hundred cases submitted for their consideration. They have only been in operation some few months, and I do not think the hon. minister need fear lest these gentlemen should run out of a job. I think that this Act should be made plain. At the last session of parliament the rate of speed at which trains were permitted to run through cities, towns and incorporated villages, where the crossings are unprotected, was increased from six to ten miles an hour. The case of McKay vs. the Grand Trunk Railway Company should be sufficient in itself to cause the government of this country to make such changes in the law as are necessary for the protection of the travelling public. This accident occurred in Forest, Ontario, where three persons were killed. An action was brought against the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It was proven in court that under the law the Grand Trunk Railway Company could not run their trains at a faster rate of speed than six miles an hour 163
ever this crossing ; yet the evidence adduced in court was that the Grand Trunk Railway Company were violating the law by running their train that day at the rate of twenty miles an hour in the village. That case was appealed from one court in Ontario to another, and the different courts in Ontario put the responsibility on the railway company and said that damages should go to the family, but when it came to the Supreme Court at Ottawa the judgment was set aside. With that condition of things existing in this country in connection with the railway law, I think it is the duty of the government to see to it at this session of parliament that the law is made so plain that where such an accident as this occurs there shall be some remedy against tbe railway company. In the town in which I live there are one or two dangerous crossings. There is a movement on foot in the different provinces of Canada to make better highways. While I am not prepared to say that at every crossing there should he a watchman or gates, I do think that on the important thoroughfares, and there are generally one or two in every town or village in Canada, the railway company should be compelled to provide watchmen and gates to protect the public. I think they should do that under the law, instead of giving discretion to the Railway Commission to say whether a watchman or gates should be provided or not. It should be taken out of the hands of the Railway Commission altogether. The law should be made plain that the railway companies should be compelled to put watchmen and gates at such crossings in order that the travelling public may have better protection. I do not think it is in the interests of the public or in the interests of the government that, in respect to any crossing where there is danger, all these regulations should be complied with which are provided for in the Act of last session, that plans should be prepared by the municipality, that profiles should be submitted, that evidence should be produced and that miles and miles of travel should be undertaken, in order to reach the Railway Commission. The Minister of Railways and the government know well that there are important crossings in this country where proper protection should be given. I believe that protection should be given and should be paid for out of the treasury of the different railway companies, and not by the people or parliament of Canada.

I understand from the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) that since parliament passed the Railway Act, 1903, a decision has been given by the Supreme Court which practically nullifies what parliament intended. The decision of the Supreme Court was that if a railway company fenced its right of way up to the highway, the company was not liable no matter at what rate of speed the trains passed over the



crossing. It certainly was not the intention of parliament to have level crossings left without some reasonable measure of protection. It is true that trains run at faster speed now than formerly, but that very acceleration of speed through crowded municipalities increases the danger. That being so, the railway companies who are responsible for the cause of that increased danger should assume the cost of giving reasonable protection at these level crossings. The minister has said, and there is some force in the contention, that the law provides for the settlement of these cases by the Railway Commission ; but the minister must know that there is a limit to the financial capacity of the municipalities, and it is a most unreasonable burden to impose upon them the obligation of coming before the commission whenever they have a complaint to make. There should be some specific provision in the law requiring the companies to give the necessary protection ; but should the companies deem such protection unnecessary then the onus of establishing that should be on the railway companies. I wish I had here the statement of Mr. Wainwright as to the obligations which were imposed upon his company in protecting level crossings, when on a recent occasion before the Railway Commission he opposed the granting of another level crossing in the municipality 'of St. Henry. Surely - when parliament has permitted trains to run at an increased speed of ten miles an hour when it formerly was six, and in view of the decision of the Supreme Court, it is the duty of parliament to obligate the railway companies to give the necessary protection. The Minister of Railways has given no valid reason why the Bill of the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) should not become law. The Railway Commission will not deal with these matters unless its attention is drawn to them. It is unfair to compel the municipalities, the lives of whose citizens are in danger, to come before the Railway Commission with plans and profiles and testimony, in order to establish an obligation which primarily should rest upon the railway companies. It would be a sensible proposition to say that upon the request of a municipality it should be the duty of tbej Railway Commission to issue an order for gates and watchmen, and that the railway company should be compelled to appear before the commission to show cause why that order should not be complied with. If the i decision of the Supreme Court interprets the law contrary to what parliament intended, then it is the duty of this parliament before prorogation to make some provision in the line of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Lincoln.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have travelled far from the real point at issue in this case.

The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada had reference to the question of the negligence of the railway company. Much stress is laid upon the question of fence protection, but in most of these municipalities there is not even an attempt made to fence along the line of railway. While hon. gentlemen have been drawing attention to that, let me draw their attention to the alternative words in the statute : ' or properly protected in the manner prescribed in this Act.' Thus the Railway Act, 1903, makes provision with respect to the protection that shall be afforded.

In view of the statement made by the hon. member for Lincoln as to the decision of the Supreme Court, how can the minister say that the Act makes any other provision than to refer the matter to the Railway Commission ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The decision referred to does not in any way affect the Act in that particular. The question was one of negligence as to whether the railway company had exercised proper care and diligence under the peculiar circumstances connected with an excursion. That does not in any way condemn the Railway Act of 1903, and more than that, the proposed amendment in no way touches the question that arose in that ease. If we adopt that amendment we would afford no other protection than to say, that there should be a watchman in incorporated towns and villages, and that then the railway companies could run their trains at any speed they might choose. Under the existing law the protection required at each crossing would be decided on its merits ; the Railway Commission would hear the evidence and determine the form of protection that should be afforded. Therefore I say that the law as it stands to-day affords the most ample protection to the public. It is much more complete than any general provision which might be enacted in the form proposed by the hon. member for Lincoln. We have the best possible protection under the provisions of the Act empowering the Railway Commission to deal with each particular case as it arises.

I have listened very carefully to the argument of the hon. member for Lincoln, and it appears to me that what he is striving for is an amendment to the law to make provision that in the thickly settled parts of incorporated cities, towns and villages, trains shall not pass at a greater speed than ten miles an hour unless a watchman is provided. Surely it will not be argued that it would not be a substantial relief to the municipalities to have that amendment made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The law now is that ' no train shall pass in or through any thickly-settled portion of any city, town or

village at a speed greater tlian ten miles an hour, unless the track is fenced or properly protected in the manner prescribed by this Act.' In cities, towns and incorporated villages there are no fences. Other sections of the Act-186, 187, 224 and 25-all contain provisions for protection.

I am not quite clear what the hon. gentleman's objection to the Bill is. other than that he is determined that there shall be no amendment. According to my short parliamentary experience, we usually first lay down the policy of the law. We have created a railway commission, and have laid down some general principles to govern that commission. It amounts to this, that the hon. Minister of Railways prefers the Railway Commission to legislate on this matter, whereas my hon. friend from Lincoln proposes that this House shall declare, by an Act of parliament, what its will is. I ask the hon. gentleman if that is not the substantial difference between himself and the hon. member for Lincoln.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I simply say that what is ample protection at one crossing Is very inadequate protection at another. Parliament at its last session delegated certain powers to the Railway Commission, very wisely I think, because that Commission can better judge, from the circumstances and the evidence in each particular case, as to the character of the protection to be afforded.
Did I understand the hon. minister to say that the provision in section 227 of the Act of 1903, with regard to fencing, in towns and villages, is not complied with ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I mean to say it does not apply in a general way, because not only do incorporated cities, towns and villages not fence, but they are very much opposed to any such thing.
My hon. friend is entirelv mistaken, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: How about Toronto, Hamilton and Brantford 1

I was directing my remarks more particularly to towns and villages. I think I am safe in saying that in every town and village in the province of Ontario the provisions of section 227 with regard to fencing are complied with.
