speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: House in Committee on Bill (No. 128), to prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes.-Mr. W. S. MacLaren. I 163 i

Might I ask the hon. gentleman who has charge of the Bill to explain the features in which this Bill differs from that introduced 12 months ago. I understood that the legislation of last year was to prohibit the sale of cigarettes to minors, but a great many members of the House who sympathize with the prohibition of the sale to minors do not sympathize with this Bill.

There is practically no change between the Bill introduced last session and the present Bill. The defect in the Bill of last year upon which the Speaker rejected it, was that it should have originated in the Committee of the Whole House. The Bill, however, was the same as this, prohibiting the manufacture and sale of cigarettes.
I was not aware that it was the same.
Yes, that is correct. .

Word for word the
same ?

That is my
impression.

I had the honour of introducing a deputation of men engaged in the tobacco trade to the Minister of Justice last year. They laid their case before him respecting this or a similar Bill, if I remember correctly. These traders expressed their willingness that a law should be enacted prohibiting the sale of cigarettes to minors ; they do not keep their establishments open for the encouragement of the sale of cigarettes to minors, but they felt that the Bill of last year would be a great injustice to them. The Bill of last year did not give satisfaction to either party, and both were invited by the Minister of Justice to make representations to him, it being thought that by the time the succeeding session of parliament was called it might be possible to prepare a measure that would give reasonable satisfaction to both parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill to which my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) alludes, was a proposed amendment to the Criminal Code, but unfortunately this present Bill has been introduced on a resolution adopted by a large majority in Committee of the Whole House.
Was not the deputation last year in reference to a proposal to prohibit the sale to minors ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes ; under 18, I think it was.

After the Bill was rejected by the Speaker, on account of an informality, the Minister of Justice proposed an amendment to the Criminal Code making it an offence under the code to sell

cigarettes to persons under a certain age. and I think afterwards the minister said that this was not acceptable to those behind this Bill standing in my name, nor were the manufacturers of cigarettes pleased with it. Is that correct ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The evil caused by the use of cigarettes by minors is recognized throughout the country, and it is beyond doubt that there is a very general desire, both in parliament and out of parliament, to prevent the sale of cigarettes to growing boys. The present measure goes very far ; it prohibits the importation, manufacture or use of cigarettes by any one. I have been a smoker for quite a number of years and I would not feel it a great hardship to be deprived of cigarettes, but at the same time, I recognize the fact that there are very many others, good citizens, who indulge in the use of cigarettes, and, as they think, without any very great injury to themselves. With the permission of the committee, I would suggest a remedy to my hon. friend. I received a letter from a very good friend who is anxious to check the evil in question. This letter, I think, embodies a principle which would most effectually prevent the evil. My correspondant says :
If the smoke debate is not ended before this reaches you, would it do to suggest that a law be enacted whereby no cigarettes can he imported, manufactured or sold in the country as now, put up and sold in packages rolled and otherwise, but in lieu thereof, that cigarette tobacco in bulk may be imported and manufactured and that pure paper for rolling the same in may also be imported, manufactured and sold in the country. That is to say, the boy would have to buy the tobacco and the paper and roll his cigarette before he could smoke it.

He would soon get on to that.
It would be of considerably more trouble to him than now.
He would soon get on to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: And the revenue officers could inspect the tobacco so sold and the paper to see that it was free from all impurities. This idea has two points to lessen the evil of cigarette smoking, and would be a law that could be effectually carried out. The dealer would not be in a hurry to wait upon a dirty-faced urchin and sell him two cents worth of tobacco and strip off the necessary paper, and tie it up with a string and give it to the boy. And perhaps the boy would spoil the paper and spill the tobacco in his attempts to roll it. The boy would get tired and so would the dealer. As it is now, the dealer can easily hand over a package or two of cigarettes for five cents. You make a law that would make them both tired and they will soon quit it.

That contains the kernel of a remedy that mignt well he applied. But, seriously speaking, while I recognize the evil, I do think that the Bill which is now being promoted by my hon. friend goes a very great length, and I, for one, would not feel like supporting it. I was not present at the time the resolution was before the committee. It is true that last session I favoured the resolution. But I did so under a misapprehension as to what it was proposed should follow that resolution.
You have had a change of heart.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am always willing to admit a mistake, and I am true to my convictions so far as I can be. I would not give a silent vote on this subject. My reasons for voting against this Bill are that it has too wide a sweep and that the law, even if passed would, in niy opinion, be entirely inoperative, because you cannot prevent the smoking of cigarettes by adults, nor would there be any general desire for such legislation.
We will try it any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I presume that it will be tried if the majority favour it. But I do not think it will be successfully tried, and I do not believe in playing at legislation. 1 do not believe that mere sentiment should rule. There are a good many people, very good people, who are in favour of this Bill. They are actuated by the highest motives, and we ought to respect them. But I think that they are mistaken as to what the law would accomplish. And, because I think the law would be inoperative, the passing of it would be simply beating the air, it would be simply an attempt to play upon sentiment. Therefore, I oppose the measure and wish to put myself on record as opposing it.

The resolution introduced last year was moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) and seconded by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). I would draw the attention of the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) to the debate of last year. So far as I can gather from a hasty perusal of the report, the object these hon. gentlemen desired to achieve was to restrict the sale of cigarettes in the case of minors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To control it.

Yes, to control it. This Bill is more sweeping than the Bill of last year. It surely cannot be seriously contended by hon. members who support this Bill that they can pass legislation that will be effective in prohibiting the importation and sale of cigarette paper to adults who wish to roll their own cigarettes. I sup-

ported the Bill last year to restrict the sale of cigarettes In the case of minors and would be glad to support it this year. But the Bill now before us Is altogether too sweeping, as I think lion, gentlemen who support it should see for themselves. Are they going to keep out cigarette tobacco and determine what may or may not be so classed 1

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And what will become of what is already in the country ?

Apart from that, it must surely be plain that adults who smoke cigarettes would procure the tobacco and the paper if necessary, and make their own cigarettes. There should be good reasons given before we are called upon to vote in favour of such a Bill.

I think the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is correct, so far as the legislation of last year is concerned, and the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) is wrong. I believe that the law introduced last year was to restrict the sale of cigarettes to minors and it was along that line that we worked. I will admit that this Bill goes further than that of last year. And, while I am prepared to support this Bill I must admit also that I agree with the members who are opposed tp it that it is impracticable to prohibit the manufacture, importation and sale of cigarettes so far as adults are concerned. But the object is to get legislation that will restrict the sale of cigarettes. I may say for the information of the House that I have been informed that in the city of St. Hyacinthe they procured provincial legislation similar in character to that which we have been trying to procure from 'this parliament. That legislation prohibits the sale of cigarettes to minors under certain restrictions. And I am told that the law is effective so far as St. Hyacinthe is concerned, and has practically stopped cigarette smoking there. I admit that this Bill goes further than originally intended, but I suppose it is introduced to meet the wishes of those who are agitating for legislation on this subject. My hope was that the ladies of the Women's Christian Temperance Union would have accepted the amendment to the Criminal Code suggested by the Minister of Justice last session. But, failing that, we are trying to secure legislation that will work out the results desired.

It is not my desire to deceive anybody as to the legislation last year I was quite sincere in what I said about it, and notwithstanding what has been said, I still think I am right. Of course, I am open to conviction. When the resolution was passed last year, and the Bill based on it was rejected, the Minister of .Justice offered to introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code making it an offence to sell cigarettes to minors under a certain age. But, what troubles me is why that should have been offered as a compromise if it was exactly what was provided by the Bill of the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Biekerdike). And we are told that this proposal of an amendment to the Criminal Code was rejected by the members of the Women's Christian Temperance Union and the tobacco manufacturers. Unless I am given chapter and verse to prove the contrary, I stick to the opinion I started out with as to the effect of the resolution of last year.

The objection made by the dealers or retailers' of cigarettes was that the person who purchased the cigarettes was not reached by the amendment. They were willing to accept the amendment if the person who, with themselves, violated the law, were required to share the punishment.

But, if the hon. member for^ West Toronto ((Mr. Clarke) will allow me, what we were discussing was the nature of the Bill of last year. A good deal of emphasis was laid upon the point, by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. liolmes) and others, that the Bill sought to be introduced last year was not a Bill for the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale of cigarettes, but was a restrictive measure with regard to the sale of cigarettes to minors. I am sti'l of the opinion that the legislation sought last year was identical with the Bill introduced this year.

I am bound to say that I agree with the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. W. S. Maclaren). I do not think there is a doubt that the Bill of last year prohibited the manufacture, importation and sale of cigarettes. What I think has caused the confusion, that it was proposed in another measure to amend the Criminal Code so as to deal only with minors; but the Bill of the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren), for which I voted and am prepared to vote again this session, was one absolutely to prohibit the sale, importation and manufacture of cigarettes ; and it was on the other matter that the discussion arose mentioned by my hon. friend for Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The matter of dealing with the Criminal Code came in as a sort of result of the measure introduced by the member for Huntingdon. The measure of the hon. member for Huntingdon was exactly of the same nature as is before us now.

As seconder of the resolution introduced last year, I desire to say that I understand the present Bill is of the same character as that introduced last year. The aim and intent of the Bill was

to preserve the youth of the country from the harmful habit of using cigarettes. We had a law in Ontario to prohibit the sale of tobacco to minors, but it was practically useless, as it was not observed in any part of the province ; therefore the Bill introduced last year, like the Bill introduced this year, was of a more drastic character and had for its purpose the prohibition of the the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes.

I would like to read a few extracts from the speeches made by the mover and seconder of the resolution which preceded the Bill that was introduced last year. These were the resolutions :
That the object of good government is to promote the general welfare of the people by a careful encouragement and protection of whatever makes for the public good ; and by equally careful discouragement and suppression of whatever tends to the public disadvantage.
That the smoking of cigarettes has been proved by overwhelming testimony to be productive of serious physical and moral injury to young people, impairing health, arresting development, weakening intellectual power, and thus constituting a social and national evil.
The legislation licensing and restricting the sale of cigarettes has not proven sufficient to prevent these evils, which will continue while the public sale of the cause of the mischief is permitted to go on.
That this House is of the opinion, for the reasons hereinbefore set forth, that the right and most effectual legislative remedy for these evils is to be found in the enactment and enforcement of a law prohibiting the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes.
Now let me read some of the observations made by the gentlemen who moved and seconded the resolution,
Were the gentlemen who voted last year voting on the resolution or on the speeches made ?

They were voting for the purpose of restricting and regulating the sale of cigarettes to minors. If the hon. gentleman will allow me to read some of the statements made by the mover and seconder, I will try to establish what I said. The hon. gentleman who moved the resolution said this among other things :
I shall only lay before the House a few of the many facts that have come into my possession to show the baneful effect of cigarette smoking upon the boys of this country. I believe tr.rc if the injury that is being done were known, there would be a unanimous vote of this House in favour of this resolution or of some similar measure. I hope I shall have the majority of this House at my back, for there are very few- men who are fathers of boys but have had more or less cause to know the bad effects of this cigarette habit upon boys.
' Mr. RICHARDSON.	,
There is no young man or boy but wishes to succeed in life. All want to get along ; all want to better their position ; success in life, in these days of strong competition, means honesty, temperance and economy. A boy or young man who has these, with good health, must succeed ; while, if he lacks them, even moderate success will be impossible. I think, Sir, we are all agreed that the boy who is addicted to the cigarette habit cannot succeed in this country unless he has a [DOT] very strong * pull ' somewhere, while the boy who is not addicted to that habit does not require any ' pull '-all he wants is the push, and he succeeds in getting to the front. I have with me certificates from the most eminent physicians throughout the country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and all these documents go to prove that the cigarette habit, with the boys at least, is very, very injurious. I think there is no hon. member of this House who will say nay to that proposition. I would be the last man on the floor to attempt to interfere in any way with the rights of the subject. Once a boy has come to the age of maturity, he has a right to do as he pleases. All I wish to do is to introduce some measure that will protect the boys from this very bad habit of recent years-for, Mr. Speaker, it is only of recent years that it has taken such a hold on the country.
Then the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) who seconded the motion, spoke on the same line. He said :
The mover of the resolution stated clearly at the outset that the intention is to reach the young, so far as it is possible, to reach those who are of immature years, those who have not attained their full physical development, those upon whom the evil effects of cigarette smoking are perhaps more apparent than they are on people of more mature years. I contend that the use of- cigarettes by children is injurious. We have not only to quote the opinions, as I will give them later on, of a number of medical authorities thereon, but I have taken the trouble to ask medical men myself since I have been in Ottawa and elsewhere as to the effect of cigarettes on children, and they assure me that their use is very detrimental indeed, detrimental both from the moral and physical standpoints, that it destroys the intellect and prevents the development of their physical nature.
I need not quote any more from these speeches because they are filled with similar arguments. The object hon. gentlemen were aiming at is one with which we all must sympathize, that is, to prevent the sale of cigarettes to the children. Those who are in the trade were willing to have an amendment made to the code provided that it punished those who bought cigarettes as well as those who sold them.

I am very pleased to find my hon. friend (Mr. Demers) and the ' Gazette ' agreeing in something. The ' Gazette ' is mistaken in the statement that there is no interest in this Bill taken outside of a very few. The ' Gazette ' would not be as apt to know regarding such a matter as I would be myself. It is not my intention to discuss the matter at any greater length. The resolution proposed last year was adopted and carried two to one in this House. The Bill was introducel by myself, went through its second reading and was carried by a majority of 128 to 52. I am content to leave the matter before the House. I am prepared for a vote at any time.

I would like just to set myself right. My hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) was right in so far as the nature of the Bill was concerned. It was a general Bill restricting the importation of cigarettes but the whole trend of the discussion was along the lines indicated by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke).
I would like to say to my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) that I think he is right about the measure introduced last session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have a copy of the Bill here.

I see that the resolution, after relating to the extent of the evil, contains this paragraph:
That this House is of the opinion, for the reasons hereinbefore set forth, that the right and most effectual legislative' remedy for th^se evils is to be found in the enactment and enforcement of a law prohibiting the importation, manufacture, and sale of cigarettes.
It was very general. The House was not disposed to vote for such a sweeping measure and I think it is a pity that those interested did not accept the proposition made by the hon. Minister of Justice that the government was ready to amend the criminal code in such a way as to prohibit the sale of cigarettes to minors under the age of eighteen. I voted for this resolution introduced last year by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) and so did the hon. Minister of Justice. But, I was convinced after the discussion that we should limit the scope of this legislation. I think it is a great pity that the suggestion was not adopted particularly in view of the very lengthy discussion that took place last year. I am ready to vote for any measure which will prohibit the sale of cigarettes to minors, and I think an amendment to the Criminal Code would certainly to a very large extent attain the object which we all have in view. The measure is evidently Mr. DEMERS.
too sweeping to have the approval of the House and under these circumstances I think it is a pity that the hon. member for; Huntingdon has introduced it. I for one afW not disposed to encourage it though I quite agree with and approve of the subject he has in view.

I do not claim to have a memory that will recall everything that takes place in this House ; in fact, I am very thankful I have not because there are many things said here perhaps that ifr is as well to forget. I have, however, a very distinct recollection in regard to the measure introduced last year by the hon. member for Montreal. St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike). It was, I believe, in the nature of a resolution which squarely set forth the fact that the object was to prohibit absolutely the importation, sale and manufacture of cigarettes. Now, that may be a very drastic measure. We have nothing to do now with the Bill introduced last year. We are dealing with the measure that has been brought before the House this year by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) and whatever the measure last year contained it will not have any special bearing upon' the vote that we will be called upon to give to-night, as to whether we are prepared now to pass a Bill absolutely prohibiting the sale, manufacture and importation of cigarettes. It may seem a very drastic measui'e, but if I can gather anything at all from the sentiment of the country as shown by the many petitions presented to this House and also * by the vote that has already been given by this House on the Bill which is now before us, on the occasion of the second reading, the sentiment of the whole country is that those who have arrived at a mature age are called upon to give up something that they might desire to practice in order to save the young generation from a habit which everybody admits is pernicious and injurious. That! seems to be the meaning of the vote that was given a short time ago and that seems to be the sentiment of the country. I have no hesitation in saying, viewing it from that light, that I am prepared to support the clause of the Bill which is now before the committee and shall vote for it as well as the subsequent clauses if they are submitted to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned. I am not caring very much whether this Bill is identical with the Bill introduced last year or not. I am under the impression that it is the identical Bill. But. we have not to do with what was introduced last session. What we have to do with now is what is before us to-night and as far as I am concerned I am anxious that the Bill now before the committee shall become law. Every one in my constituency

with whom I have spoken is exceedingly anxious that this kind of legislation shall be passed. I am firmly of the opinion that this is the kind of legislation that the women of the Women's Christian Temperance Union are anxious to see passed; through this House. One hon. gentleman tried to make it appear that the fact of this Bill being before the House was merely a joke. I can assure that hon. gentleman that if he had a son. if he had a young boy whose health was undermined, whose mind was being destroyed and whose physicians had told him that the continuous smoking of cigarettes was the cause, I do not think, if he were the father of a son1 of that kind, he would think this very much of a joke. On the contrary, he would think it something that this country should take, seriously into consideration. In my own town the habit of cigarette smoking prevails to a tremendous extent. I do not know that there is. a town in the country where the habit of cigarette smoking has made such tremendous strides within such a short space of time. In supporting this Bill I have the sympathy of the teachers, the preachers, and the leading people of my constituency who are anxious that this Bill should become law and therefore I shall be pleased to support it.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say one or two words upon this subject before the vote is taken. I regret very much that my hon. friend from Huntingdon has introduced a Bill which goes, in my opinion, altogether too far. It does not seem to me that there is any more reason for totally prohibiting the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes than there would toe for applying the same prohibition to the manufacture and use in all forms of tobacco. I presume that everybody practically admits that the use of cigarettes by growing boys is calculated to affect their nervous system and in some cases, if carried to excess, to undermine their constitution and ruin their health. Last year when this question was before the House, I was very much impressed by the dispassionate statement by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Roddick), who pointed out very clearly from medical testimony of the highest character that the use of cigarettes by young people was injurious. But. on the other hand he stated with equal emphasis that as far as the medical profession was concerned they did not consider the use of cigarettes or tobacco in any form in moderation to be injurious to the average man. For my part, I do not believe in the efficacy or in the utility of trying to make men good by Act of parliament. I believe that if hoys are going to be trained in the way they should go you should not propose to come here and do it but that you should go''into your own home to do it and if occasion needs, spank the boy instead of endeavouring to put upon the statute-book legislation which would be carried out more in the breach than in the observance. It does not inure to the dignity of this parliament or to the respect which the people ought to have for the law to enact legislation of that kind, and I think my hon. friend would have done far more good if he had limited himself to an effort to place on the statute-book an Act restricting the sale of cigarettes to young people. For my part I cannot perhaps set my face against all the testimony but I go about the country a good deal, I keep my eyes open and I fail to see such an enormous consumption of cigarettes as some hon. members in this House pretend to see and as some of the people who have petitioned us claim to exist. I have nothing but kind words to say of the good women who have taken it upon themselves to push this movement. I believe they have a perfect right to do it but I believe that their fears have been excited, that they perhaps have gone too far and that they exaggerate the extent of the evil, because in the rural parts of the province of Quebec the sale of cigarettes is almost unknown. I hardly think my hon. friend from Huntingdon is an authority on this question, for I believe he is a non-smoker himself, but I can tell him that you can go into any store in the Amer-scan cities and buy ten little cigars for a dime, and they are not such bad cigars either.
What are they made of ?

They are not too bad : I have smoked them myself. One of the arguments used as to why we should prohibit cigarettes is because they are so cheap that the small boy with five or ten cents in his pocket can go into a tobacco or drug store and buy a package, but suppose this law should be passed, and even suppose it should be enforced, then it is reasonable to assume that the ten cigars for a nickel will take the place of ten cigarettes for a dime. For my part, I would be strongly in favour of something like the amendment to the Criminal Code introduced by the Minister of Justice last year. I think that goes far enough, although I am afraid that there might be some difficulty in enforcing even such a provision. I understand that /anti-cigarette legislation has been passed in a number of the states of the union, but I have never seen any proof advanced here or elsewhere that it has achieved the results hoped for by those who exerted themselves to have it placed upon the statute-book. I regret that any boy should use cigarettes even moderately ; indeed tobacco in any form should be used by young men only in great moderation, because in these days of keen competition it requires all the energy and all the nerve force our young men possess to enable them

to win in the battle of life. Unlike a good many of my fellow-members, I have not to go back upon the vote which I gave last year. I believe that a targe number of hon. gentlemen voted last year for this resolution believing it to be a joke, or at all events believing that it would never reach a serious stage in the deliberations of this parliament, and now they have to reconsider their votes.

I do not look upon this as a joke, nor have I from the start. I took no part in the debate last year, and I do not see why the women of the Women's Christian Temperance Union asked me to take charge of the Bill this year ; but they did, and I at once consented. I did not know much about the matter at the time, but I have given it some thought since, and I can say that I am more in earnest about it now than I was at the start. I am thankful to the members who to-night have spoken so kindly in regard to these ladies who have charge of this matter, though I must say that in a former debate they were not so gently dealt with. There are 404 branches of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, having about 12,000 members. East year some hon. gentlemen who spoke about these ladies suggested that they should start cook ing schools. I want to know who it is that carry on the cooking schools throughout Canada at the present time. If the hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Osier), who referred to the cooking schools last year, would look around him he would find that the ladies who were carrying on the cooking schools in the Slums of Toronto are the ladies of the Women's Christian Temperance Union and the Young Women's Christian. Association.
And in the absence of my hon. friend (Mr. Osier), I may say that there is no more generous supporter of that movement in Canada than he is.
And probably the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclaren) might administer a rebuke to the Prime Minister, who repeated the same language.

I do not suppose the remark was intended to be offensive in either case. At all events, I know that these women who are advocating this Bill are acting in the best interest of the young people of Canada. I believe that there is a law in everyr province except Quebec prohibiting the sale of cigarettes to youths, but I do not think it has been found to be effective, and that being so, it was thought that it was necessary to have what is called the more drastic legislation incorporated in this Bill.

The argument is very stale, that you cannot make people better by Act of parliament. If that argument were carried into effect, then the greater part of our Criminal Code would not be in existence. We know that there is a genera-Mr. PARMELEE.
tion of young people growing up at the present time, feeble in intellect, feeble in constitution, feeble in growth, and this altogether owing to the use and abuse of cigarettes. Those who oppose this legislation are people who use tobacco, and who probably use it to no good purpose. The best minds in this Dominion owe the member for Huntingdon a debt of gratitude for introducing this Bill, and he is supported by the best Christian people in the Dominion. Whether this Bill becomes law or -not, its introduction affords proof that there is a party in this parliament who are anxious that this evil should be removed. I have great pleasure in supporting this Bill, and I would be delighted to see it become law. I can tell the House that if it does not become law this session the force of public opinion will cause it to be placed on the statute-book before long, and hon. gentlemen will find that their vote to-night will become a live question when they next appeal to the people.

I believe in the principle of this Bill, but at the same time I am inclined to think that it is too broad in its scope, inasmuch as it would prohibit adults who are accustomed to the use of tobacco from smoking it in this form. I believe that every effort should be made to prevent our youths, those under the age of eighteen let us say, from using cigarettes. Should they not smoke until they attain that age, it is no more than likely that they may refrain from cigarette smoking ever afterwards. Even if this Bill should become law. there are various methods by which its provisions could be evaded. If the Bill went so far as to prohibit the use of tobacco in any form by young men under the age of eighteen years, or even under twenty-one years, I think it would be more beneficial. I read the other day the statement by a magistrate whose duty it was to try juvenile offenders -for various forms of crime, and he claimed that out of 500 whom he tried 90 per cent of those convicted had been addicted to the use of cigarettes. In view of such strong evidence it behooves us to use every effort to prevent boys under the age of eighteen from using tobacco in any form. It is my opinion that a great deal can be done by clergymen and by those public spirited women, who have taken a great interest in this matter, and who are deserving of a great deal of credit for their efforts towards the protection of our young men. If they were to form an anti-smoking society amongst young men, and if the employers of labour joined with them in making a rule that they should not engage young men who used cigarettes or tobacco in any form, a great deal of practical good would be accomplished. I merely make this suggestion in the hope that the women, if they have not thought of if in the past, may consider it seriously, and adopt a method of that kind.

Section agreed to : Yeas, 50 ; nays, 27.
On section 2,
2. No cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers shall be imported into Canada or entered for consumption therein, and all cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers, or papers intended as such, shall be subject to seizure by any officer of customs or inland revenue ; and they, with the packages in which they are contained, shall be subject to be seized and forfeited to His Majesty, and shall be disposed of under regulations made by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the people of this country are to be told;, by formal Act of parliament, that children of any age may use tobacco in aiiy form except in the form of cigarettes. That, I understand, is the effect of the legislation which we are now passing. I cannot concur in that.
I think the important objection to this provision is the impossibility of carrying it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will create a race of hyprocrites.

The question is what are cigarette papers or cigarette wrappers. A great deal of the paper used for cigarette wrappers is merely paraffine paper which is used for putting up powders, and can be got in any drug store in the country. Ordinary cigarette paper is rice paper ; but where rice paper is used once, I venture to say that paraffine paper is used a dozen times, and it can be got at any drug store and can be put up by any one. So that it seems to me that it is impracticable to enforce this Act, because it is impossible to detine what is cigarette paper. Half a dozen kinds can be used for the purpose.

If parliament is to protect the children of this country against the evil of smoking cigarettes, we should have an amendment made to the Criminal Code such as was attempted by the Minister of Justice last year. He failed in that attempt because neither party was satisfied. If the gentlemen who support this Rill would unite in asking the Minister of Justice to frame an amendment to the Criminal Code so as to punish not only those who sell cigarettes but those who purchase them for the use of minors, that would be a practical measure which I think would be effective. To prohibit the importation of cigarette paper and to allow the cigarette tobacco to be imported and sold seems to me to be a fatal defect in this Bill. We all agree that boys ought to be prohibited in some way7 from smoking cigarettes, and I think such an amendment to the Criminal Code would go far to put an pnd to this great evil. You must punish both the purchaser and the vendor if you want an effective measure. I would suggest that the
gentlemen promoting the Bill will unite in asking the Minister of Justice to frame an amendment to the code which will carry out the object which these very estimable ladies have in view.
I agree with the hon. member's suggestion that an amendment should be made in the Criminal Code to prohibit the sale of both cigarettes and cigarette tobacco to minors.

I have only to say that I am not the maker of the Bill. It was framed at the request of those promoting it, by a firm of solicitors in this * city. After it was placed in my hands, I submitted it for my own satisfaction to [DOT] another firm of solicitors in whom I had confidence, and they endorsed it. If the feeling of the House is that it should be amended in any way, we will argue the amendment ; but so far as the Bill is concerned, it is my intention to push it through to the end ; and after it is made law or defeated, if the Minister of Justice can then frame an amendment to the Criminal Code to suit both those promoting this Bill and those opposed to it, I will have no objection.
Mi-. FITZPATRICK. I should then be asked to make something criminal which it would be impossible for any one to do if this legislation passes. It seems to me tlpit we should be informed what is the object which those promoting this legislation have in view.

1 understand that in every province except the province of Quebec, restrictive legislation was passed. It was found that that was not effective in reducing the use of cigarettes. I am not a lawyer, unfortunately ; I suppose that if I was I might be able to argue these. law points with lawyers, learned in the law, but I am advised that this provincial legislation was not effective and that in fact some questions as to the constitutionality of the provincial Act arose after that judgment given on the Lord's Day Act. When those in favour of such legislation found this provincial legislation practically a dead letter and not enforced-, they thought they would take a stronger measure and secure the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale.
Then I understand the object is to prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
How far are you going in that direction by this legislation, Mr. Chairman ? The tobacco can be introduced into the country and you are prohibiting the importation of cigarette paper or cigarette wrappers. Now

what is cigarette paper or a cigarette wrapper ? Is there anything in this Bill to define them ? How are you going to reach the people who introduce the paper into this country from which cigarettes may be manufactured ? You should supxily a definition of these words so as to be able to proceed against any person who imports it. After all we are not here simply to enact legislation for the mere purpose of putting it on the statute-books. Let us see what we accomplish by what we do. I want to see how far by the aid of this Bill the object in view would be accomplished.
. It cannot be accomplished by the Bill in its present form and if it cannot be accomplished by the Bill in its present form why should we waste our time on it ?

The Minister of Justice has said that the aim, no matter what the wording of the Bill of last year might be, was to provide legislation to protect the children of this country from the injurious effects of cigarette smoking. Let me quote again one or two sentences in support of what the Minister of Justice has said to show that. The mover of the Bill (Mr. Bickerdike) last year said :
Once a boy has come to the age of maturity, he has a right to do as he pleases. All I wish to do is to introduce some measure that will protect the boys from this very bad habit of recent years.
That is the statement of the hon. gentleman who proposed the resolution last year. The hon. gentleman who seconded it was equally to the mark and equally clear. He said :
We are not arguing from the standpoint of those of mature years, but from the standpoint of the bearing of this question on the youth of Canada.
There is a consensus of opinion, it cannot be questioned, that the excessive use of cigarettes is disastrous, physically, morally and mentally to children, and every one will sympathize with legislation, that will mitigate that evil. I believe that can best be done by an amendment to the Criminal Code as suggested last year by the Minister of Justice. But the Minister of Justice pointed out afterwards that this legislation had not met with the approval either of those who desired to restrict the sale, or of those who were engaged in the manufacture and sale of cigarettes. It was pointed out by dealers that while they could be punished for selling to minors, those who came in to induce them to break the law escaped scot free.
That is no argument.

It is a practical argument. It has been' found in connection with the Ontario law that there are adults who are mean enough to purchase cigarettes for children and give them to children. It has been done again and again. It would not Mr. FITZPATRICK.
be fair under those circumstances to hold the dealer alone responsible. If the person who aids the child in purchasing the cigarettes was made amenable to law there would be_ a strong forward movement in the direction we desire, but this legislation will not accomplish its object, and that is the reason T oppose it. If we pass this legislation the tobacco will be rolled into cigarettes by some one, and the children will continue to use them.

I am not an expert on tobacco and I would like to ask if there is any difference between cigarette tobacco and ordinary cut tabacco ?
Mr. AaRKE, It is much finer, as the hon. gentleman knows.
A gentleman behind me says no.
I speak of course subject to correction ; I am uot a cigarette smoker ; but I am satisfied that tobacco is specially made for cigarette use.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Whether it is or not yTou can use it.
It does not affect what I said, because if any kind of tobacco can be rolled into cigarettes, we are not accomplishing anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand the injurious effect of cigarettes results from the paper used in their manufacture, not from the use of tobacco. We admit that tobacco is not noxious in itself. It is allowed in every form but we are here saying that cigarettes are not to be used because of the paper used in connection with their manufacture. What are we doing ? That paper which is supposed to be deleterious when used for the purpose of manufacturing cigarettes, is not to be imported, but any other deleterious paper, even if it is absolutely noxious may be imported and may be used. What do we mean ? W'hat are we trying to get at ? It seems to me we are not serious iu this matter.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are serious ? Then, we are incapable because we are not accomplishing the object we have in view.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice. When the question of the liquor Bills came up before parliament and was referred to the Privy Council the question of jurisdiction was at issue. I would like to ask the minister whether the Dominion parliament can prohibit the sale of cigarettes. I understand the provincial parliaments have passed the prohibition laws, and I would like him to explain whether the prohibition of the sale of cigarettes comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial parliament or of the Dominion parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is any question about that. I think there is no doubt about our power to pass this legislation.

Might I ask the member who has the Bill in charge (Mr. Maclaren) whether he has any information to the effect that any serious effoi't has ever been made to enforce the laws on this subject now in existence in Nova Scotia, and if so what is the nature of that information ?

I have no information as regards Nova Scotia. I have as regards Ontario. They have tried to enforce it there but since this judgment on the Lord's Dav Act there has been a good deal of feeling 'in regard to the question whether the legislation passed there was constitutional. There have been prosecutions in connection with the local Act but I cannot say how far they have gone or what, success there has been.

It seems to me that it has been made abundantly clear that for the present time this is not an effective measure, and will fail to bring about the results desired by those supporting it. For my own part I have no very strong convictions with regard to the manufacture, sale, and use of cigarettes ; am not a user of tobacco. But if I read this statute correctly I am satisfied that the passing of this Act is not going to prevent the boy of this country smoking cigarettes, and it is for this reason I think that this measure should not become law. If we are serious about this matter let us introduce legislation that will be effective. Those who are earnestly desirous of accomplishing reforms -I am myself desirous that they should be brought about-should introduce only measures that would be effective, not half effective in bringing about tlie results desired.

Might it not be better for the Minister of Justice to give us the aid of his judicial mind in making this Bill perfect and not be raising legal and technical objections against it ? The majority of this House is m favour of this Bill, and' he admits that it is not perfect m its present form. Then let him, by his experience and his judicial mind, give us the assistance he can to make it perfect.
With mv lion, friend's permission, I would like to ask him a question. In his judgment, are the majority of this House opposed to the importation and manufacture of tobacco m any form ?	[DOT]
Judging by the vote given here to-night, there is a decided opinion of the House in favour of the Bill, and I would desire to see the Bill made more perfect.
But I am talking about tobacco generally ?
I am like my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Alexander Johnston) and do not use tobacco in any form, and I believe that the world would be much better if nobody used it.

I had not intended to speak on this Bill, but in view of the discussion that has taken place, I would like to say a few words. I am not a cigarette smoker, but I do enjoy tobacco through the medium of a pipe or cigar. I know how I should feel if legislation were being introduced, or attempted to be introduced, to deprive me of the pleasure I derive from smoking my pipe ; and those who prefer taking tlieir tobacco in the form of a cigar-rette, I think, have an equal right to object to our placing any restriction upon their liberty. I quite agree with the principle of applying the Act so far as concerns children under a certain age. But, for one, I do not think any person has the right to say that a man who is of age and capable of judging for himself shall not smoke cigarettes, any more than he has a right to say that a man shall not eat certain kinds of food. You might as well legislate in one way as in the other, for there are certain kinds of food that are harmful to certain constitutions, just as cigarettes are, and one can ruin his constitution by over-eating as well as over-smoking. I presume that the object of those who support the Bill is to stop the smoking of cigarettes in Canada. If I understand the King's English, this Bill, if passed, will have no such effect. By this Act we simply prohibit the sale of the cigarette, in its manufactured state, and also prohibit the importation of proper cigarettte paper. There is nothing here with regard to tobacco. You can bring in the cigarette tobacco and use any paper-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Newspaper.
As the hon. minister suggests, you can use newspaper, or you can use a brown paper that may answer the purpose instead of the regular cigarette paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You can poison all the children in the country with it.

There is no question about it, the Bill will not have the effect that the promoters of it desire. As to what was said by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Win. Ross) that the Minister of Justice should suggest amendments, I do not know that that is what the Minister of Justice is here for.
He condemns the Bill.

As I condemn the Bill, because it is a useless Bill. After all, the argument used in support of this Bill is that it will protect the children. Well, so far as that is concerned, I support such legislation, but I believe the best way to embody

it is in the amendment to the Criminal Code which the Minister of Justice offered last session to bring in. But, as to making this applicable to grown men, I believe that object cannot be effected, and so I shall vote against the Bill.

I have received several petitions from my county from that worthy organization that has been several times referred to, the Women's Christian Temperance Union. I may state here what I said in answer to the petitioners, to whom I gave my reasons why I would vote against this Bill. I sympathize with the object of these ladies, and my reasons for opposing this Bill is that if I helped to enact such a law, I should be helping to do the very contrary of what they really want. I go further than some of the opponents of the Bill and say that this will not prevent the use of cigarettes by young men, but it will develop the habit of smoking bad cigarettes by young children. As an opponent of the smoking of cigarettes by children, I will vote against' the Bill, because X know by experience that when boys cannot get cigar-rettes made with proper paper, they do not buy their tobacco in the form of a small cigar, as one hon. gentleman mentioned, but they buy the cigarette tobacco, and wrap it for themselves. As everybody knows the obnoxious effect of cigarettes is not produced by the tobacco, but by the paper, and so, in France, for example, where the manufacture of cigarettes as well of cigars is under the control of the government, they have very careful analyses made of the paper for cigarettes by chemists of the school of science. And the result is that, of all the cigarettes used the French and the Belgian are the least obnoxious. What is proposed here is not progressive legislation, but the most retrogressive legislation that well could be. I will vote against it because I am in sympathy with the movement started by the Women's Christian Temperance Union, and which the hon. member for Huntingdon is in good faith supporting and which I believe will be defeated if this Bill should pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as I am concerned, I am opposed to the use of tobacco by children in any form. I am likewise opposed to an attempt being made to interfere with the liberty of individuals. If it is legal for a man to use tobacco in his pipe or in the form of a cigar, I see no reason why those who do use it in that form should say that a cigarette smoker should be prevented from using it in the form he prefers. That is the second objection. And the third objection is that this Bill defeats the very object the hon. gentlemen have in view. Instead of aiding the children, you would put in their hands cigarettes of inferior character, you will oblige them to use a cigarette which will be very much more deleterious in its effects than the cigarette now sold. If we are in earnest in this matter and if we are considering this Bill seriously, some answer should be given to these objections.

I understand the force of the remark made by the Minister of Justice. But what troubles me in connection with this matter is that before cigarettes were introduced in this present form there was not the same use of tobacco by people of tender years. They did not make cigarettes in those days, when they had just as much fine paper to do it with and just as much fine cut tobacco. When those cigarettes were brought in in this particular form, and put into a nice little box with a picture on it, then the use of cigarettes began. I think if you asked 100 boys of this country how they commenced to use tobacco you would find that 90 per cent of them, perhaps 99 per cent, would say that they commenced with the use of cigarettes. Now before these cigarettes came iu they did not roll them up in this way. Probably now that people have got a taste for fancy cigarettes they will follow it up by making them out of all kinds of dirty paper. But to my mind, driving out cigarettes as made in the country at the present time, I am satisfied will diminish the use of tobacco by those of tender years, and that is why I am supporting this legislation.
Section 2 agreed to, yeas 39, nays 25.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is easy to be virtuous at the expense of your neighbour.
On section 3,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Surely we have reached the limit. Before sending people to jail for a year, I hope some one will tell us what is meant by cigarette paper. If it is to be a crime incurring a fine and imprisonment for a year to import cigarette paper, surely we ought to be told what is meant by the words ' cigarette paper.' The time has come when we ought to consider whether we are in earnest or not.

I believe that the one who ought to be punished is he who being addicted to the cigarette habit, would refrain from smoking cigarettes in the future, because he is afraid he is going to be fined. It is an axiom of natural law that nobody is bound to obey an unjust law. Therefore, instead of placing upon the statute-book such a penalty as is suggested, it should be enacted here that any one who, being addicted to the cigarette habit, abstains from smoking cigarettes, because he is afraid of breaking the law, shall be liable to be fined.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will some one please give us information to enable us to understand what is meant by cigarette paper. Is there any such legislation as this on any statute-book in the world ? Where is such legislation as this to be found ?
I am not so familiar with the statutes as my bon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all very fine, but the hon. gentleman ought to be familiar with what he is trying to do. Surely we are entitled to some information about it.
The Minister of Customs will define that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not the Minister of Customs. Any magistrate in the country may send a person to prison for a year, any- country magistrate.
We merely- declare what the law prohibits.	[DOT]

There ought to be some definition of a cigarette in this Bill. I am a habitual smoker of cigarettes, one of those sad examples of stunted growth. I think for the sake of public protection we ought to have cigarettes defined. I do not, as a rule, buy them, I make them with my own hands-I do not know whether I would be . considered as a manufacturer or not. But unless there is some definition of what is a cigarette, I think the Bill is very misleading. A cigarette of the same size as the ordinary cigarette, is made with clear tobacco, the purest kind of tobacco and no paper at all is used in its manufacture. Now is the law to exclude such an article ?

Let us consider this matter seriously. Take section 3 of this Bill-there is no definition of what a cigarette is in the Bill, there is no definition of what cigarette paper is in the Bill. Now who is to decide ? We might have on the bench a magistrate who is a perfect crank, opposed to smoking in any form. A person is charged with selling some paper which is termed cigarette paper-who decides that ? There is no definition in the Act itself. It is left to one man who, as I say, may be a crank on the subject, left to him to decide whether there is a contravention of the Act or not ; and in his hands is placed the power, on his own interpretation, of sending a man to prison for a year. I think we ought to consider what we are doing before we go any further. At all events, if we are going to pass this Bill, let some person who is fathering the Bill, or supporting it, propose some amendment to define what cigarettes and what cigarette papers are. Let us not put ourselves at the mercy of any man who may be sitting as a magistrate to say that the liberty of the subject may be taken away for a year because that magistrate considers that a certain brand of paper is cigarette paper.

It seems to me that some hon. gentlemen are going very far in trying to frustrate the object of this legislation. An Act was passed here a little while ago applying to traders, and when I asked what the word ' trader ' meant, I was
told that a court and jury would define that. This Bill is to the same effect. We are making an act a criminal offence, and we are now told we ought to define what certain things are. Some hon. gentlemen are more particular now than they have been in respect to other matters. I am particularly anxious to pass this section as it stands. If we cannot accomplish the absolute prohibition of an evil that everybody wants to see destroyed, at least we can take a step m the direction of accomplishing it. If we can at any time accomplish it we ought to do so in the interest of this country. It will not do any harm to stop the importation of this material with that object in view and if people are going to be so afraid that they are going to punish for importing cigarette paper because of the want of a definition of it in this Bill the less will be the material imported out of which boys can make cigarettes.
They can buy it at any store.	*	[DOT]
This House lias de-dared in favour of this measure.
Not yet.

It has declared in favour of the measure or we would not have been in committee on it. It has declared in favour of the resolution, it has declared in favour of a Bill founded thereon and it has gone into committee on the Bill. It has declared that cigarettes shall not be imported, manufactured, or offered for sale. If we are going to enforce the sections which have been declared passed by two votes in this House to-night, in order to be consistent we must adopt this section which declares that cigarette paper and wrappers shall not be imported. If we are going to be consistent, if we are going to back our own action, not only last session, but this session, and this night, we must pass this section in order to carry out the tw'o previous sections.
Mr. GALLIHER, The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), when we find him expressing opposition to any Bill, does not want to be cut off short. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I submit respectfully after all possible consideration and in all earnestness the question if it is consistent with our dignity to pass legislation in the hope that that legislation may subsequently be frustrated by the action of the Senate. I say that it is not consistent with the dignity of the House that we should take such course as that. I do not want to repeat that because I am not quite certain but that there are some members who are not present in the House to-night who are in the hope that if this legislation goes through this House it will never get through the Senate. Let us try to realize what this means. Take this clause here for instance ; for a second offence if a man happens to sell a cigarette after having been fined once, he goes to jail for a year without the option of a fine. Do we realize what that means ? For a second offence he goes to jail without the option of a line. I do not know that there are any offences on the statute-book in connection with which such a penalty as that is enforced. Is it conceivable that we are going to father legislation imposing such a penalty as that ? [ In the next place do we realize what this >
Mr. GALLIHER
means ? What is going to become of the investors of this country who have entered into the manufacture of cigarettes ? What is going to become of those who have their supplies of paper, tobacco and machinery on hand ? What this means is that we are going deliberately to expropriate the property of these people and in some cases practically ruin them and give them no compensation. They started their industry with the sanction of the law and here we are now without a moment's warning introducing legisltion which will destroy this industry. Do we know what that means ? Are we thinking what it means ? Are we in earnest in passing this legislation ? Surely we ought to reflect upon it. Surely we ought to consider it. It is not conceivable that this legislation is going through and that we are not going to provide some compensation for those whose industry will be affected by it.

There is another side to this question that ought to be considered. The object we are aiming at will never be obtained by this kind of legislation. We will make it impossible to get remedial legislation in the near future. This Bill may even pass the Senate-I do not know whether it will pass this House or not- but it has only to be enforced to be repealed. It is a pernicious Act which cannot be enforced. The people of this country will not stand for it when they understand what it means. I say that with the greatest possible respect, because every lion, member in this House has a right to vote as he sees fit, just as I have ; but if the aim of this Bill is to protect the children of this country, it will fail and make that protection much more difficult to provide in future. We have pointed out again and again that the large vote given for the legislation introduced last year was because of the distinct pledges of the mover and seconder of the resolution that their aim was to protect the children of this country from indulging in the use of cigarettes. We could all sympathize with a measure of that kind. Here we have a Bill which proposes to send a man to jail practically without even a fine-a cruel proposition emanating from such a source, an unchristian proposition, if I may apply the term ; and I repeat again, Mr. Chairman, that if the object is to provide legislation to mitigate the evils which undoubtedly follow from the too free use of cigarettes by minors in this country, this legislation will fail and be a barrier in the way of obtaining effective legislation from parliament. I say that with the greatest possible respect. I will not take up any more of the time of the committee, but I would not be doing my duty if I did not enter my protest against the passage of legislation of this kind.

A blank is very often left in a Bill to be filled in with the

length of time that a man has to serve who breaks the law, or the amount of fine that he has to pay. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What has the hon. gentleman got to say as to expropriation without compensation ? That is a new principle of legislation in this House. We; are to expropriate the people engaged in this industry and we are not to give them any compensation ; that is a novel departure.

I am surprised to hear the Minister of Justice, who ordinarily displays great judgment on questions brought before the House, using such an argument. No man in this country goes into business without taking risks.
No.

Yes. If the ar'gument of the Minister of Justice is good, he should remember that you destroy the cigarette business to a limited extent if you make it apply to minors, and as a large proportion of the cigarettes are smoked by minors, then when you prevent minors smoking you destroy the cigarette industry to a large extent, and the Minister of Justice is willing to do that without compensation. I do not believe that this idea of compensation for vested rights will hold water. Parliament cannot be restricted as to the legislation it shall pass within its powers, and if parliament thinks it right and proper to pass such legislation in the public interests, it can do so without there being any just claim for compensation. This proposed legislation has been before the House for months, and if there were any- serious intention of guarding the youth of Canada in this respect, we might have heard something about it before this. There is sufficient public opinion in this country to demand legislation of this kind, at all events so far as it is applicable to minors. I am free to concede that perhaps this Bill goes too far, but failing to get legislation to protect the minors we try to get all we can.

The Minister of Justice introduced legislation last session amending the Criminal Code so as to protect the minors of Canada from cigarette smoking. Why was not that legislation supported then ? The hon. member (Mr. Holmes) says that failing to get that, he wants this general Act, but it is not the fact that he has failed to get legislation protecting minors. I for one would support 164.
such legislation as would also, I believe, the majority in this House.
Why doesn't the Minister of Justice bring it in now ?

I cannot answer for the Minister of Justice. Notwithstanding the opinion of the member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) the question of vested rights does enter into the question. It is true in one sense that any one engaging in a business takes risks, but it is not true in every sense, and I would like to know how my hon. friend (Mr. Holmes) would like it, if legislation were passed here preventing him from publishing his newspaper. When a man enters into business that is sanctioned by the laws of the country, he should not take the risk that parliament will wipe out that business without at least giving him compensation ; and it does not matter whether he is a newspaper publisher, a grocer, a whisky seller, or a tobacconist. If you commence to apply the principle of destroying vested rights in an established business without compensation, where are you going to draw the line ? I believe that this question has not been considered seridusly enough by those supporting the Bill.

Why don't you propose an amendment to make it right ?
Mr, GALLIHER. Some of you who are so anxious in support of this Bill; why don't you get up and move an amendment which will make this legislation effective ?

You are a lawyer and you ought to know how to make) the legislation workable. If you are sincere, why don't you propose an amendment and if it appeals to my judgment I will support It ? Why does not the hon. gentleman propose some amendment that will remedy the grievance, that he feels so deep down in his heart to-night ?

There are questions involved in legislation of this kind which deserve the most careful consideration from this parliament, and in all candour I say that some of the hon. gentlemen who are supporting this Bill do not seen!" to have seriously considered what its effects will be.

There is considerably more in the question of compensation in connection with this Bill than some people seem to realize. My hon. friend from West Huron had probably in mind a prohibitory liquor law without compensation when he ventured his opinion to-night. The liquor business is carried on under a system of license, but the retail commerce in tobacco, and in dry goods and in all the other branches of trade is not licensed. People have been invited to invest their moneys in this legitimate enterprise ; it differs from a business which is licensed, inasmuch as in the



latter case you invest your capital with your eyes open knowing that you are only specially privileged under that license which may be withdrawn at any time. There is a great deal of capital invested in cigarette manufacturing in this country ; there is the machinery, the tobacco bought, the contracts made for the future, and the employment of labour. I am not personally interested as to whether this Bill shall pass or not. I agree with other gentlemen that there should be an absolute prohibition of the use of all kinds of tobacco so far as minors are concerned, but even if this law were passed I could manufacture a cigarette myself without any breach of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With reference to compensation, we must bear in mind that factories for the manufacture of cigarettes are licensed by the government; therefore, the people carrying on that business have been authorized by the government to invest their money in the factory and machinery, and then by legislation of this sort we come along and wipe the whole thing away. You license them to do a certain thing, and they pay a license. When you cease to license them, they have no more authority to manufacture.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend confounds two things which are very easily distinguished. I am dealing with a legitimate business. The government might take away a license from the manufacturer, but that would not prevent his machinery being valuable to him. If you license him to carry on a business, you enter into a tacit contract with him that you will give him the protection of the law in carrying on that business. Then you come along with this Bill and destroy his business. The case put by the hon. member for South Wellington was that of a stationer or druggist carrying on a business over which this parliament has no control. He has paper of a certain description and you declare that he must not sell it. He has bought it when the law said he had the right to buy it. You say he must stop selling it and must destroy it. If the paper is found in his possession, he is liable to a penalty. So long as this parliament is content to pass legislation of that sort, the responsibility must rest on those who want to be virtuous at their neighbours' expense. According to this legislation, a man may have his pipe or cigar, but the man who enjoys his cigarette is not to have it. Where is the justice in legislation of that sort ? A remark fell from the lips of one hon. gentleman on the other side of the House which showed what is being done. The hon. gentleman said that the ladies who want this-

legislation passed have not thought of the consequences of it. I am sure we are not old ladies, though we may be acting as such. After all, why should we allow ourselves to be stampeded into legislation of this sort, simply because a cry has been raised in the country which never was intended to be translated into legislation such as this ? What the Women's Christian Temperance Union and the other ladies had in view was to prevent the sale of cigarettes, and tobacco as well, to minors. That is a laudable object and something which we can advocate. I will hold up both hands for that. 1 introduced a Bill last year to prevent the sale of cigarettes to persons under eighteen years of age, but the majority of this House were opposed to it, and those interested in the business were opposed to it also. If we mean to take over the parental authority exercised by parents over their children, if we have abundance of time for that, let us apply it as we ought to apply it. If I have spoken on this Bill more frequently than I usually do, it is because I honestly think this legislation reflects discredit on the House. Perhaps I am wrong in that, because the majority say so. But I think it is not to our credit to have legislation of this sort, the parallel of which is not to be found on any statute-book in the world.
Mr. FOWIjER. I understand that the Minister of Justice is perfectly satisfied to have restrictive legislation so far as the sale of cigarettes to minors is concerned. It has been pointed out that minors are the principal consumers of cigarettes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am standing for individual liberty.

We all stand for individual liberty but not all for individual license. A great many people make the mistake of confounding liberty and license. I think the Bill should pass as it is. I see no difficulty in the way and I am satisfied to have it passed.

I do not think that the Minister of Justice has any right to assume that any member is supporting this Bill with the understanding or expectation that the Senate will throw it out. I have heard no such remarks in the House, and the minister has no right to suggest that any member will do other than his duty. The Minister of Justice points out defects in the Bill, but there is no man who should be more capable than he to offer amendments to the Bill that will perfect it. That is his duty, a duty that rests upon him more particularly as a member of the cabinet than upon any other member of this House. The cabinet is responsible for the legislation that passes this House whether it is of a private or public character. If it is defective it is the less to their credit. Mi1. L. P. DEMERS. In answer to the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) I would say that he made a great mistake in saying that no indemnity should be given. This is a property. These people have invested their money in manufacturing cigarettes, and the manufacture is a property and we cannot deprive them of their property without compensation. Ownership is defined in the Civil Code which is in force, in Quebec, as follows :-
Ownership is the right of enjoying and of disposing of things in the most absolute manner, provided that no use be made of them which is prohibited by law or by regulation.
Surely then the manufacture of cigarettes is an ownership, a property recognized by law. The manufacturer is not using it in a manner prohibited by law, or regulation. The money invested in that property is an ownership recognized by law.
Another paragraph in the code says :
No one can be compelled to give up his property, except for public utility and in consideration of a just indemnity previously paid.
What are we doing here ? We are taking over the property of a man, what he owns, legitimate property for public utility and if we do so, we must give him the indemnity that should be given. That is the law of France, the law of England, the law of Canada, the natural law, and we are violat-

Ing all these laws in order to deprive the citizens of this country of a natural right. I contend that this parliament has no right, nor has any parliament, the right to deprive me of a natural right. You have not the right to prevent me drinking what I like, or smoke what I like. All of these laws are abuses of power, and the duty of a man, if he is worthy of the name, is to violate them, when they come into force because they are against the liberty of men.
