I think the mover of the Bill should accept the suggestion that in the meantime, before another session, he might consult with the representatives for example, of the Chinese of the Russian government, for I think those are about the only countries where similar legislation could be found. As the legal authorities on both sides of the House have been unable to tell us in what way this legislation could apply, how you could define the offence, and therefore how a judge could apply the penalty, I think surely the hon. members who are responsible for this legislation should get proper information from the only semi-civilized countries in the world where similar legislation has been adopted, before it is put in force in this so-called free country.

I would like to say a few words before this motion is put. In the first place, this Bill is badly drafted. In the next place the effect of this Bill will be to make this House utterly ridiculous throughout the world. I presume the promoters of this Bill desire to prevent young men from smoking cigarettes, but at the same time, there is not one word in it to the effect that only young men will be prevented from smoking cigarettes. The result is that as the Bill stands at present the man who smokes one-fifteenth part of an ounce of tobacco will be sent to the common jail for one year, while the man who smokes one-eighth of an ounce of tobacco will be left free. Can we insert such an illogical clause on our statute-book ? As

pointed out by the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa), it is utterly absurd, utterly ridiculous, to insert in our statute-book, this illogical discrimination between the man who smokes a little bit of tobacco and the man who smokes half a pound, the first one being sent to jail and the second one being left free. Under the circumstances I should vote against the Bill. It cannot be amended, it is altogether bad, it is anticommercial, it is immoral, There is no proof that the smoking of tobacco is bad. Tobacco has been in use for centuries, and I have not been able to find, either in philosophy or ethics or medicine, that it is wrong to smoke tobacco. Why should we accept the word of the promoters of this Bill as the word of the gospel ? There is nothing in the gospel against tobacco. For my part I am not willing to take the word of the promoters of this Bill as gospel. Let me say to my hon. friend from West Huron (Mr. Holmes) that it has not been proved that tobacco is a poison. It is no worse to smoke tobacco than it is to use hundreds or thousands of other articles that are in common use in this country. Therefore I say that the aim of the Bill is bad, the Bill itself is bad because it does not discriminate between classes of persons who are to suffer through the application of the Bill. Then X say that the penalties imposed by the Bill are too heavy. For all these reasons I should vote against the adoption of the Bill, not only against this fifth clause, but I am opposed to all the other clauses which have already been adopted by the committee.

I think those who are opposed to this Bill are going pretty far. They are assuming that all the wisdom in this House is confined to those who are opposed to this Bill, and that those who are supporting this legislation are a lot of incompetents, who really do not know what they are doing. I think it is assuming a little too much. I do not know but those who have voted for this legislation are quite equal in intelligence to those who have voted against it. I have nothing to be ashamed of in connection with this matter. I am in earnest, I think this is good legislation, and I suppose those who are supporting the Bill think it is good legislation. I think that hon. gentlemen go rather far when they try to put us down as a lot of people who don't know the gospel, and who don't know much anyway.

The Canadian Association of Masters and Mates has been troubled over this matter a great deal, the travelling public, that is those who travel on steamboats have been troubled a good deal about it. The Canadian Association of Masters and Mates finding that the matter was of such importance, and finding apparently that no move was going to be made by the government to remedy the evils of which they complain, met at Toronto last winter; on February 8th, 9th and 10th, and passed resolutions in regard to it. I am speaking from the book entirely when I say that this legislation is absolutely required. It is all very well for some officer in the hon. gentleman's department to tell him that it is not. He has not run steamboats on the lakes. He does not know one-quarter as much about it as the Masters and Mates Association of the Dominion of Canada do. This association would not have passed resolutions asking that the law be amended unless these amendments were necessary. I quote from the minutes of the meeting held in Toronto on February 8th last, this resolution :
Captain Milligan moved, seconded by Captain Jordan, that the Dominion government be memorialized to amend the law so as to make the examination of masters and mates more rigid and to require that all recommendations of a master to a candidate for examination must be made on oath, or the candidate must produce a recommendation from the executive of a branch of this association.
That is the first amendment which my Bill deals with. It requires that the evidence under which a certificate may be issued shall be given under oath. At present part of the qualification of a candidate is that he must have served under a certain master on inland waters for a certain time, and obtain a certificate to this effect. The master, in a great many cases, does not like to refuse, although the candidate may not have compiled with the conditions, and so he gives the certificate, but if he had to swear to it he would not do so. There is no responsibility on the man who makes the statement ; he commits no criminal offence, but at the same time he deceives the department and the public.

I cannot accept that.
I am sick and tired of having it suggested to me that public Bills should go to special committees for the purpose of having them defeated and not considered on their merits. maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
Then I will go on. As I have said, the first amendment is in regard to the evidence being under oath. The Minister of Marine says this might be made a matter of regulation, but this constant government by Order in Council is merely taking away the right of parliament, which is to make a law which every one is bound to carry out, and which cannot be altered from time to time. The second amendment is very important, and it deals with the nationality of masters and mates sailing Canadian ships. In the United States one must be an American citizen before he can be master or mate of any boat owned in the United States ; and, therefore, it is that in boats plying side by side in the same waters the American boat must have an American captain, whereas the captain of the Canadian boat need not be a British subject. This is unfair, and it should be remedied. An American citizen can come into Canada and get a boat, which otherwise would be commanded by a Canadian, but before a British subject can command an American boat he must become an American citizen. The
Masters and Mates Association have dealt with this subject in the following resolution :
Moved by Captain Milligan, seeconded by Captain Jordan, that this association memorialize the Dominion government to cancel all certificates of masters and mates held by persons who have gone, or may go, to the United States and obtain certificates to sail vessels, where such persons are required to swear allegiance to the United States in order to qualify them to obtain such American certificates. .
That is the recommendation of the Canadian masters and mates with regard to that. It seems to me that I should only have to state this case to get the unanimous support of this House for this measure, except that of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who seems to think it ought not to pass. The case is so obvious that it looks to me like an insult to the intelligence of this House to argue that a man who is not a British subject should be allowed to come into Canada and take away from masters and mates who choose to remain British subjects their occupation, and at the same time to say to Canadian masters and mates that they shall not have a similar privilege in the other country. The next amendment I wish to make is :	[DOT]
No person shall be entitled to present himself for examination for master until he has obtained a certificate of competency as mate, and has served as such for at least twelve months, and furnishes a statutory declaration of the master under whom he served of such service.
I wish to add that to the section which deals with that matter. That is recommended also by the same association which deals with it in this way :
Waiting the arrival of the St. Catharines delegates an informal discussion took place as to the administration of the law respecting certificates to masters and mates. Instances were given in which certificates of competency were granted to a number of persons who had served as pursers and in other like capacities, but who had no knowledge of seamanship whatever and never sailed a boat. No person should be granted a certificate as a mate unless he had served twenty-four months as wheelman and no one to be allowed to take masters' papers unless he has obtained a certificate of competency as mate and has served as such at least twenty-four months.
The next amendment I wish to make reads as follows :
No person shall be entitled to present himself for examination as mate until he has served as wheelman for the period of twenty-four months, and furnishes to the examiner a statutory declaration of the master under whom he served of such service.
These are the two sections which are dealt with in the resolution which I have just read. Now I come to a matter which it is a wonder to me has not been amended long ago. Nobody, however, noticed it. It

is a matter which should only require to be stated in order to have this House correct it. It will hardly be believed by hon. members that the men who are examining candidates for masters' and mates' certificates do not require to be qualified themselves. Anybody can be appointed an examiner for masters and mates in inland waters. All up through these lakes, which are considered more dangerous than the Atlantic ocean, because the storms come up more quickly, and there is less sea room, men who should be most competent are allowed to pass examinations held by anybody whom the government appoint, and who need not know anything about the subject. It is just as if lawyers were to be examined by dry goods merchants or carpenters or blacksmiths, or any other men who do not know anything about law. Perhaps the hon minister will say that the government would not appoint a man who was not a competent lake master. But it is just as well for the government to have the law behind them, so as to enable them to resist successfully the importunities of persons who might want the appointment in return for some political service. The government should not appoint as an examiner any one who is not himself a competent lake navigator ; and it is well for the government to be strengthened by the law on the subject. That matter is dealt with also by a resolution of the Canadian Association of Masters and Mates passed on February 8th of this year, at the city of Toronto. It seems that to-day a collector of customs is the examiner of masters and mates ; and this motion is in these words :
Moved by Capt. Crawford, seconded by Capt. Gidley, that we petition the Dominion government to rescind the Order in Council which makes collectors of customs examiners of masters and mates, and the amendments to the law to provide for the statement of qualified examiners who shall be paid a stated salary instead of by fees as at present ; the examiners to be appointed to be in all cases competent lake navigators.
Following out the recommendation of that resolution, I have this amendment in mv Bill :
Section 4 of the Act respecting Certificates to masters and mates of ships is amended by adding after the word * examiners ' in the sixth line the words ' which shall be by salary, and not in any way affected by the number or results of the examinations,' and also by adding after the word ' effect * in the last line the words ' but no person shall be appointed an examiner in respect to masters and mates of ships trading on the inland waters or on coasting voyages unless he himself is a competent lake navigator and has a certificate to that effect.'
Under this nobody could be an examiner who was not a navigator. We have the additional almost ridiculous state of affairs, that the examiner is paid fees, and it is his interest to pass the man who seeks to be Mr. LANCASTER.
examined, and as a result he may drown people instead of carrying them safely. The Bill provides that the examiners shall be paid salaries. There are only two men in the province of Ontario to-day who would be examiners. One lives at St. Catharines, and the other I believe is generally found at Toronto. The Auditor General's Report show the fees they received last year. I am told by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that it is his intention to have these gentlemen salaried. I am simply carrying out his intention in this Act. Since this Act has been printed and before that time, the minister told me verbally and in a lettter that it is his intention to make these officers salaried officers, although they are not salaried at present. Then why should he oppose this amendment ? It is in the interest of public policy that examiners should not be affected financially by the fact of those who come before them for qualification passing or not' passing. That is the only way in which we can expect proper examinations and care in results.
The next amendment is that:
The section substituted for section 7 of the said Act by section 2 of chapter 41 of the statutes of 1891 is amended by adding after the word ' boats ' in the fourteenth line the words ' such certificates to be conditioned to become void upon " the holder thereof renouncing his allegiance to the British Crown." '
That is auxiliary to the carrying out of what I have contended for in regard to British subjects. If a man gets a certificate and afterwards ceases to be a British subject, by going to the United States or any other foreign country and becoming a naturalized subject of such country, then his Canadian certificate as master or mate should be of no value.

Therefore you cannot give them the quality necessary to bfe>
masters and mates.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext: There is no flag in Canada other than the British Flag. If they are naturalized Canadians they are only naturalized British subjects. There is) no other citizen of a British country than a citizen of Great Britain and Ireland. There may be a Canadian but he is a British subject. If he is qualified to hold any position in Canada it is because he is a British subject. Surely the Minister of Justice does not contend that Canada can have citizens who are not subjects of Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext: I contend as a most elementary legal principle that you cannot confer upon a foreigner the rights of a British subject. You can give him certain rights but not the rights of a British subject ; that js within the exclusive jurisdiction of the British parliament.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext: We can certainly say who shall be masters and mates on our vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
Yes, we can do that.	.
Mr, LANCASTER. If we say ' British subject ' does not that include Canadian citizens. Is the Minister of Justice not a subject of Great Britain, am I not one. is my boy in St. Catharines, born in Grimsby, in the county of Lincoln, in the Dominion of Canada not a British subject ? If I was goingi the length of saying what should make a man a British subject for the purposes of this Bill that would be different, but I am simply saying that no matter what constitutes a man a British subject, if he is one he is qualified to be a master or mate of a British vessel. The government of the United States will not allow a man who is a British subject and a Canadian citizen also to run a boat there, and we should protect our masters and mates and see that Americans are not allowed to come oven here and take their situations. For illustration. If an American master should come over to St. Catharines and obtain command of a Canadian boat, putting a Canadian out of his place, and if that Canadian should go to Buffalo and try to get the place vacated by the other man he could not do so because he was not an American citizen. An American, however, could go from country to country in alternate years in this way, commanding first an American and then a Canadian boat, but as the Canadian is a British subject, he Is limited to taking the boats he could get in Canada and if the. other man was willing to take $10 a month less, and put him out of his position then the Canadian would not be able to get a boat in the United States. If you want to protect Canadian workingmen and the people of Canada you should see that their boats are run by Canadian citizens and British subjects. The statute that I propose to amend is chapter 42 of the statutes of 1894,
section 4, which Act itself amended the Revised Statutes relating to the certificates of masters and mates. This section now reads :
Examinations may be instituted in Canada for British subjects or persons domiciled in Canada for at least three years.
So, the word ' British subject ' is used in the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext: The question is whether we can make British subjects in Canada.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
What is meant by the word 'British subject' in this statute? It is strange, what new, technical objections are raised, now to statutes that have been left unquestioned for years. This statute was passed in 1894, and the Minister of Justice, if not actually Minister of Justice all the time, has been in power since 1896. Yet, he has not changed the section of this Act. For my part I am prepared to take chances on whether a British subject is a Canadian citizen or not, or whether a Canadian citizen can be anything but a British subject. The statute provides that examinations can be instituted for British subjects and those are the fellows I want. The Minister of Justice and I need not quarrel about what the word ' British subject ' means. The statute provides that the examinations may be instituted for British subjects or for persons domiciled in Canada for at least three years. I want to strike out the words * or for persons ' in the second line. So, it would read :
Examinations may be instituted in Canada for British subjects domiciled in Canada for at least three years.
So, the Minister of Justice must not blame me for using the words 'British subjects ; my amendment does not contain these words at all. I did not put those words in the statute and all I am doing is simply not taking them out of it-I can leave them where they have been ever since 1894. It seems to me that the amendment I propose is not only in the interest of navigation generally and of all who travel in steamboats in Canada. The section in full reads :
Examinations may be instituted in Canada, for British subjects or for persons domiciled in Canada for at least three years who intend to become masters or mates of ships trading on the inland waters of Canada, or on the minor waters of Canada or on coasting voyages, or who wish to procure the certificates of competency or service hereinafter mentioned ; and foreign subjects serving in ships registered in Canada, and trading on the inland waters of Canada, or on the minor waters of Canada, or on coasting voyages,

shall be deemed to be domiciled in Canada while so serving.
So, under the present statute, while working here a foreign subject can get the benefit of the three years' residence, under my amendment, he cannot get the certificate unless he becomes a British subject. 1 am supported here by the resolution moved by Captain Milligan that I have already read. There was a further resolution :
Captain Gidley moved, seconded by Captain Dix, that a committee composed of Captains Milligan, McCoppen and Boyle, St. Catherines, be appointed, with Mr. Lancaster, M.P., for Lincoln, to revise the Act relating to masters and mates, prepare amendments to said Acts in the shape of a Bill on the line of the resolutions passed and suggestions made at this meeting, and that it he presented at the coming session of parliament.-Carried.
In response to that request I met that committee on several occasions, they being good enough to come to St. Catharines to see me. They requested me to put the matter into shape, and so I have put it in legal phraseology in this Bill. It was gone over carefully, and after it was printed it was gone over again just as carefully. I am authorized to say that the Bill I am advocating is in every particular exactly what the Canadian Association of Masters and Mates want. Now, in case any hon. gentleman should charge me with carelessness in not ascertaining the facts as to who can be a mate or a master in a United States vessel, I will refer to the revised statutes of the United States, sections 2165 and 2174. I need not trouble this House with the former, because it merely sets forth what a man has to do in order to become a eitizen of the United States. But section 2174 provides as follows :
Every seaman being a foreigner who declares his intention of becoming a citizen of the United States in any competent court and shall have served three years on board of a merchant vessel of the United States subsequent to the date of such declaration, may on his application to any competent court and the production of his certificate of discharge and good conduct during that time, together with the certificate of his declaration of intention to become a citizen, be admitted a citizen of the United States ; and every seaman being a foreigner shall after his declaration of intention to become a citizen of the United States for the purpose of manning and serving on board any merchant vessel of the United Stafes, anything to the contrary in any Act of congress notwithstanding, hut such seaman shall for all purposes of protection as an American citizen he deemed such after the filing of his declaration of intention to become such citizen

	-

speechtext: Does that mean that they are to be citizens of the United States ?

speechtext:
The time referred to is the time he has served on the vessel of the Mr. LANCASTER.
United States-three years-and on application and production of his certificate of discharge and good conduct-

He then becomes a citizen of the United States and can vote. He becomes a citizen of the United States by making a declaration of his intention and by serving three years on a United States vessel. But no British subject who is going to remain a British subject will go over there and declare his intention of foreswearing Great Britain and sailing in an American vessel for the purpose of doing it. Now, here is the statement of the United States local inspectors, dated March 12, 1904, and signed Frederick L. R. Pope and Joseph H. Sckumocher. They are the United States local inspectors, and are attached to the Department of Labour and Commerce in the United States. They write this letter, addressed to Mr. W. D. In reply to your second question, an Act of congress approved May 28, 1896, provides that, after the 1st day of January, 1^97, no person shall be qualified to hold a license as a commander or watch officer of a merchant vessel of the United States who is not a native born citizen or whose naturalization as a citizen shall not have been fully completed.
That is the present law of the United States. So, that on aill grounds it seems to me these amendments I propose ought to be adopted. I trust the House will see that no harm can be done and a good deal of good may be done to the travelling public by adopting these amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
As I stated just now, there is no necessity whatever for passing this Bill during this session. We have received no serious complaints yet in the department. The only difficulty about the Act is that it has been amended so many times that it needs' consolidation, together with some slight amendments. I gave instructions to the chairman of the examiners to prepare a consolidation of the Bill, but unfortunately he was called away to some other business. He informed me in the beginning of May that he could not go on with the consolidation. Therefore, on the 3rd of May, I wrote the following letter to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), explaining to him that the effect of amendments he proposed could be carried out by regulations. I do not know why the hon. gentleman persists in pushing this Bill in face of the promises that have been made to him, and in face of the fact that most of his amendments are already provided for in the law now existing. For the information of the House I may read that letter, which covers the whole ground :

Ottawa, 3rd May, 1904. Dear Mr. Lancaster,-In my letter to you of the 22nd March I notified you that the amendments you proposed to make to the Masters' and Mates' Act would be embodied in a new Act which is being prepared in my department, and considering there is nothing in your amendment which calls for urgent legislation I think you might rest satisfied with my pledge. Unfortunately, owing to a heavy pressure of work, the new Bill which I propose to introduce will not be ready in time for this session of parliament. You must understand that a Bill of this nature requires most careful consideration, and if I were to decide upon introducing it this session, before every clause has been duly thought out, the result would probably necessitate the passing of several amendments in the near future.
There are reasons why I am not disposed to allow your amendment, the principal one being that you wish to introduce a great deal of matter into the Act which belongs exclusively to the regulations.
In the first section of your amendment I take it that it is your desire to obtain a more definite guarantee of applicants' service than at present exists, by requiring that their testimonials should be sworn to. This is a question of proof of service, and as such belongs to the regulations to be decided upon by the Governor in Council. New regulations will be issued when my Bill has passed, and in this respect they provide a better arrangement than you propose, namely, the production of official discharges.
Referring to the second part of the first section of your amendment, your desire to exclude foreigners has also the effect of disqualifying British subjects other than those domiciled in this country, that is to say, officers and men serving on ships registered in Great Britain or any part of the British dominions except Canada would not be entitled to examination. Perhaps you are not aware that our foreign-going certificates are recognized by the Imper.nial Board of Trade and any British possession declared by order of Her Majesty in Council under the provisions of the Merchants Shipping (Colonial) Act of 1869, as equivalent to their own, but only on condition that we adopt the same regulations with regard to the examination of candidates. In my new Bill I provided that only British subjects are qualified for examination.
In subsection 2 of section 2 of your amendment you again deal with matter pertaining to the regulations and for which there is no place in the Act. Twelve months' compulsory service as mate with a mate's certificate which you desire, is provided for in the new regulations, but with this difference, that official discharges are required in place of a statutory declaration.
In subsection 3 of the_ same section you are again encroaching on the regulations by providing that certain service as wheelman will be necessary to entitle an applicant to a mates' examination. This grade of wheelsmen mentioned by you if allowed to pass would disquanify apprentices, seamen, mates, boatswains. pursers, pilots and masters, all of whom have every right to claim examination. The twenty-four months' service you desire is 'provided for in the new regulations.
In section 3 of your amendment you have again borrowed material from the regulations to place in the Act, which, in my opinion, is . quite unnecessary and superfluous as tending to curtail the powers of the Governor in Council. No less than eight examiners are at present on salary and eventually I intend to put them on the same footing, that is to say, when the chief examiner assures me that the salaries can be earned. In the second part of this section you require that no person shall be appointed an examiner of coasting and inland waters' candidates unless he is himself a competent lake navigator and has a certfi-cate to that effect. You do not appear to be aware of the fact that a lake navigator is incompetent to command a vessel in the coasting trade. My new Bill provides that not only shall the examiner hold a certificate but he is required to pass a satisfactory examination before two other examiners to show his competency to examine candidates.
Section 4 of your amendment requiring certificates to be so conditioned that they become void in the event of the holder renouncing his allegiance to the British Crown, is too unreasonable for me to countenance. A certificate once gained is the property of the holder and has been duly paid for, and like any other property he may own must belong to him unless he has committed some crime which renders its forfeiture necessary.
The same objection applies to section 5 of your amendment.
I made just now a proposition to the hon. gentleman to have this matter referred to a special committee of this House, along with another Bill ; so I think it is quite unreasonable. under these circumstance, to pass this Bill, especially when there is no urgency for it.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
The lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Piv-fontaine) has in the closing words of ins speech given the whole reason for sending this to a special committed. The hon. gentleman said that my hon. friend's Bill is quite unreasonable. What does he want to send it to a committee for ? To shirk the responsibility that he would assume by refusing to take up this measure in this House, absolutely that is the reason. The hon. gentleman declares that a master or mate may not be a British subject and that if a master or mate ceases to be a British subject he may still retain the rights of a British subject and he is not willing to have the proposals of my hon. friend crystallized into the. legislation of Canada. The hon. gentleman proposes to have one measure of justice meted out to Canadians who go to the other side and to have a different kind of treatment for those who come from the other side to this country. The hon. gentleman says there is no demand for this legislation. There is no demand because the hon. gentleman is not in the mood to take up such legislation. The hon. gentleman thinks it is sacri-

lege that he should pass any legislation In this House which interferes with the regulations of his department. I will venture to say that the letter read here to-night was prepared by his own deputies or officers. Everybody knows that the hon. gentleman does not know anything about it. I am not doing the hon. gentleman any injustice when I say that. We all recognize that he is new in his department. I am not reflecting in the slightest on the hon. gentleman in saying that he cannot master these things in a day, but it is perfectly apparent from the letter which the hon. gentleman has read that he has red tape in his department. The hon. gentleman is content with that system of red tape which grows up in the department here. Every man knows that the time comes when we have entirely changed conditions, outgrowing that state of things, and we therefore should make changes when it is necessary to do so. What was rather astonishing was the attitude of the hon. Minister of Justice. He says that we are now attempting to declare who shall be a British subject. That is a most extraordinary declaration as far as It bears upon the legislation of this House. For all the purposes for which a man may become a British subject in Canada provision is now made. In regard to the franchise, is there any question as to whether we can make a British subject or not ? These are only some of the pretexts that hon. gentlemen will offer in opposition to such legislation as this. I think there is one plain, necessary rule that can be laid down in Canada, and that is, that a Canadian has a better right in this country than any alien has. If any man who has been a Canadian or who is a British born subject and who alienates his right by becoming a citizen of a foreign state, desires to come back to Canada and to exercise the rights to which he was born, he may become a British subject again by naturalization, which would place him in the same position as that which he occupied before. He should become a British subject before he should be permitted to exercise the right of a Canadian. Let us take the example of the country to the south of us. I am not finding fault with the system which prevails there. I think the people to the south of us are rather to be applauded for the decided preference which they have shown for their own people. If there is anything that solidifies and builds up a country, if there is anything that has a tendency'to make people attached to their country, it is that they shall have that protection in their own country that citizens of other countries receive from their own state. I do not think that this is a Bill that requires any elaboration. My hon. friend from Lincoln who has introduced the Bill has stated in the most concise terms what he proposes. One of the things which he proposes, and it is not a Mr. CLANCY.
matter to be settled by regulation, is that the examiners shall be qualified persons, that they shall be paid and that there shall be no inducement to pass candidates. That is not a matter of regulation and if it were one, if we are to judge at all even by inference from what the hon. minister has stated, it would be a very loose sort of regulation. .It is not a matter of regulation as to whether a master or mate shall be a British subject. Th'e hon. minister has declared in the most emphatic terms and he crystallized it in that letter which he has now embalmed on ' Hansard ' that he does not think that the candidate ought to be a British subject. He says he would not consent to that. Does he propose to send this Bill to a committee to ask Canadians to stifle that proposal and to let him out of the responsibility of saying that masters and mates shall not be Canadians or British subjects ? When I use the word ' Canadians ' I mean Canadians in the broadest sense. I do not intend it to be confined to persons born in Canada. One might be a Canadian born in Canada and not a British subject. He may have been born in Canada and taken the oath of allegiance to a foreign state. If he- does that he forfeits his rights. I do not for one moment believe that the hon. gentleman will take the responsibility of standing in the way of giving effect to so reasonable a Bill, and I do not believe he will have the support of hon. gentlemen on that side of the House if he does so.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CERTIFICATES TO MASTERS AND MATES OF SHIPS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is carried there are two or three words that I should like to say about this Bill. If I understand this Bill correctly the experience and ability of the men who are to navigate our Canadian ships are in no way interfered with. Every precaution surrounds the procedure introduced into this Bill by my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster), to secure that in future none but qualified mariners shall navigate our vessels. The necessary qualification for a person before he can pass an examination as master is that he shall have served twelve months as mate and that before he is qualified to pass as mate he shall have served twenty-four months as wheelsman, and he must produce a certificate from the master on the vessel on which he served ns wheelsman to that effect. What the public are interested in is that the men who have charge of our Canadian ships shall be competent. My hon. friend relaxes no provision existing in the law now. He does not interfere with the qualifications of the men who are to navigate our Canadian vessels. They must be men of experience and ability. The other provision that he asks shall be incorporated in the law is that the men who navigate these ships shall be Canadians or British subjects. He has given abundant reasons why that amendment should be

made in the law. If there were a dearth of skilled mariners there might be an objection taken to an amendment of that kind, but that objection has not been urged by the- Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine), and it cannot be urged by any hon. gentleman who knows anything about navigation upon the lakes. There is only a limited number of vessels in Canada. There is an ample number of qualified men to navigate these vessels and my hon. friend asks that preference shall be given to Canadians. I think he is quite right in asking that that amendment shall be made. It is not fair to Canadian mariners that American citizens should come over here and qualify themselves by passing the Canadian examination to take charge of Canadian vessels, who. in after years, may go back to the other side and take command of American vessels.
The law as it exists places Canadians ini a secondary position to American navigators. I cannot for the life of me see what solid objection can be advanced by the Min-, ister of Marine to the passage of this Bill. If there were a dearth of qualified Canadian mariners to navigate our vessels on the 'great lakes that might be given as a reason, but that reason does not exist. Our navigators are not permitted to navigate American ships, and It is most unfair to American labour, that foreigners should be permitted to come over here when it suits them, and take the command of Canadian vessels at probably lower wages than our, own people would want. The hon. gentle-, man (Mr. Lancaster) is entitled to the thanks of the Canadian marine for his efforts to promote this measure ; the responsibility for defeating it rests with the government and their supporters.
